Chiral Quantum Groups and Holography

Local operations, duality and reconstruction

Raeez Lorgat · 16 November 2026

The objects studied here are associative chiral algebras of configuration complexes. They are not Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras. They are augmented, coherently associative algebras for a specified configuration convolution: the augmentation ideal vanishes at the empty configuration, and the bar coalgebra factorizes on the prescribed separating opens. A Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebra instead has a chiral Lie operation on a differential module. Its passage into the associative word theory takes Chevalley chains, restricts the resulting coalgebra to monotone collisions and consecutive cuts, and then applies associative cobar. The empty algebra unit and the local field vacuum are distinct.

A boundary of a quantum field theory supports measurements of its own. Local fields can be inserted at different points, combined while separated, and brought together through singular limits. Line operators can meet the boundary or connect boundary conditions. The question of holographic reconstruction is how much of the independently defined bulk theory these boundary observables and their operations determine.

There are substantial reconstruction theorems on precise domains. Connected ordered bar and cobar give an equivalence without a cohomological boundedness restriction. Under the specified smooth realization hypotheses, nonrational affine examples reconstruct every ordinary unbounded line module and identify its exact image. Spectral quantum groups have compatible fields and level-dependent coproducts. Ordinary geometric coefficient systems recover their original chiral algebra. Current operations, analytic sewings, numerical Gaussian states, Hall correspondences and arithmetic traces provide further independently defined constructions, each with its stated hypotheses.

The remaining comparisons ask whether these structures reproduce the prescribed physical products, interfaces, bulk actions and states. An equivalence of underlying complexes need not preserve a product; a separated comparison need not extend across a collision; a full trace need not determine a state algebra; a normalized state need not determine its amplitude line or the state prepared by a geometric filling. The chapters develop the actual maps and their strongest known scopes before stating the exact open questions. The atlas provides a second route to the same mathematical constructions and sources.

Part I Observables, representations and localityChapter 1 of 18

1

Boundary observables and reconstruction

A boundary of a quantum field theory supports measurements of its own. Fields can be inserted at different points of the boundary, multiplied when their positions are distinct, and brought together through singular limits. Line operators can end on the boundary or connect one boundary condition to another. The reconstruction problem asks how much of the bulk theory is determined by these boundary observables and their operations.

The word operations is essential. A list of states, a partition function or an algebra at one point records only part of the information. We also need to know how observables combine as their positions vary, how they act on line operators, how two boundaries are joined, and how a state assigns amplitudes to the resulting expressions. A proposed reconstruction must compare these structures with structures defined independently in the bulk.

The programme’s associative chiral algebras are not Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras. They are augmented, coherently associative algebras of configuration complexes for a specified convolution. Their augmentation ideals vanish at the empty configuration, and their bar coalgebras factorize across the prescribed separating opens. Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras have a chiral Lie operation on a differential module. To obtain an associative word object from one, take its Chevalley coalgebra, restrict its collision maps to monotone surjections and its coproduct to consecutive cuts, and take associative cobar. A quantum-group structure further needs a compatible coproduct for a tensor combining systems at the same positions; that tensor and its interchange with configuration multiplication are additional data.

There are several mathematical constructions to compare. A bar construction reorganizes an algebra in terms of its relations and higher relations. A derived centre records compatible operations on its modules. A boundary field theory supplies observables, products and line operators by geometric and physical means. These descriptions can agree in particular regimes, but their names do not define a comparison between them. The main questions concern the actual maps, the domains on which they exist, and the operations they preserve.

    1.1 Reduction must retain the measurements

    The need for this extra structure already appears before quantum field theory. In a gas, pressure and temperature describe large-scale measurements without specifying each molecular trajectory. Elasticity describes displacements at scales large compared with atomic separation. In a low-energy field theory, one may integrate out modes above a chosen scale while retaining their contribution to interactions among the remaining modes. Each description chooses observables and a regime of accuracy; none is justified merely by having fewer variables.

    An exact finite calculation separates two operations that are often confused: removing a variable from the notation and integrating over its fluctuations. Let xx be a measured displacement and yy an additional displacement coupled to it. In units in which the action is dimensionless, take

    S(x,y)=12ax2+cxy+12by2,b>0,ab>c2.S(x,y)=\frac12 ax^2+cxy+\frac12 by^2, \qquad b>0,\qquad ab>c^2.

    Here x,y,a,b,cx,y,a,b,c are real. The inequalities make the quadratic form positive. Let ℏ>0\hbar>0 control the scale of fluctuations, and use ordinary Lebesgue measure. At fixed xx, the weight remaining after yy is integrated out is

    Zy(x)=∫ℝexp⁡(−S(x,y)ℏ)dy.Z_y(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}\exp\!\left(-\frac{S(x,y)}{\hbar}\right)\,dy.

    Completing the square gives

    S(x,y)=b2(y+cbx)2+12(a−c2b)x2,S(x,y) =\frac b2\left(y+\frac cbx\right)^2 +\frac12\left(a-\frac{c^2}{b}\right)x^2,

    and hence

    Zy(x)=2πℏbexp⁡[−12ℏ(a−c2b)x2].Z_y(x) =\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\hbar}{b}}\, \exp\!\left[ -\frac{1}{2\hbar}\left(a-\frac{c^2}{b}\right)x^2 \right].
    (1.1)

    The result retains two pieces of information: the effective stiffness a−c2/ba-c^2/b and the factor 2πℏ/b\sqrt{2\pi\hbar/b}. The stiffness agrees with aa when c=0c=0, and the factor can equal one at particular parameter values. Setting y=0y=0 would leave e−ax2/(2ℏ)e^{-ax^2/(2\hbar)} and omit these two outputs of the integration. Substituting the conditional mean y=−cx/by=-cx/b gives the effective quadratic form but does not perform the fluctuation integral.

    The same distinction appears when the eliminated variable occurs in an observable. Its conditional moments are

    ⟨y⟩x=−cbx,⟨y2⟩x=c2b2x2+ℏb.\langle y\rangle_x=-\frac cbx, \qquad \langle y^2\rangle_x=\frac{c^2}{b^2}x^2+\frac{\hbar}{b}.
    (1.2)

    The second term in ⟨y2⟩x\langle y^2\rangle_x is the variance. Replacing yy by its mean loses it. Thus an exact reduction includes a rule for transporting observables, not only a new expression for the action.

    For a polynomial f(x,y)f(x,y), write this rule as conditional expectation:

    ℰ(f)(x)=Zy(x)−1∫ℝf(x,y)e−S(x,y)/ℏdy.\mathcal E(f)(x) =Z_y(x)^{-1} \int_{\mathbb R} f(x,y)e^{-S(x,y)/\hbar}\,dy.

    It is linear and preserves the constant observable, but it is generally not multiplicative. Equations (1.2) give

    ℰ(y2)−ℰ(y)2=ℏb.\mathcal E(y^2)-\mathcal E(y)^2=\frac{\hbar}{b}.
    (1.3)

    An effective theory therefore needs to explain how products are transported. In field theory the analogous correction is a contraction of fields. With many insertions, the corrections must also agree when the same reduction is performed in different orders.

    The factor in (1.1) poses another question. It cancels from normalized expectations at a single fixed value of the parameters, but it matters when unnormalized amplitudes are compared, when parameters vary, or when two pieces of a theory are glued. In an infinite-dimensional field theory, the corresponding determinants and their phases need their own definition. A theorem about normalized correlations is consequently different from a theorem about the vacuum amplitude.

    1.2 From products to local operations

    Ordinary multiplication takes two elements of an algebra AA to another element:

    m:A⊗A⟶A.m:A\otimes A\longrightarrow A.

    For local observables, positions are part of the input. On a complex curve with coordinate zz, a field associated with a state aa is written Y(a,z)Y(a,z). It is an operator-valued formal series; its coefficients act on the state space. If aa and bb are inserted at distinct points zz and ww, their product can have a pole as zz approaches ww.

    The basic current example has singular part

    J(z)J(w)∼κ(z−w)2.J(z)J(w)\sim \frac{\kappa}{(z-w)^2}.
    (1.4)

    The symbol ∼\sim here records only the terms singular at the diagonal z=wz=w; it does not assert equality of the complete product with the displayed function. The number κ\kappa is the central coefficient of this current algebra.

    Even this one pole has two different expansions. In the region |w|<|z||w|<|z|,

    1(z−w)2=∑n≥0(n+1)wnzn+2,\frac1{(z-w)^2} =\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)\frac{w^n}{z^{n+2}},

    whereas in |z|<|w||z|<|w|,

    1(z−w)2=∑n≥0(n+1)znwn+2.\frac1{(z-w)^2} =\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)\frac{z^n}{w^{n+2}}.
    (1.5)

    They describe the same rational function on different domains. In formal algebra, the domain is replaced by a prescribed order of Laurent expansion. Changing that order is a mathematical operation; it cannot be suppressed by writing both series as the same completed tensor.

    This is one reason to formulate local products geometrically. The configuration of distinct points is an open subset of the Cartesian power of the curve. Its complement consists of collision diagonals. A local algebra must describe products on the open subset and their permitted behaviour near those diagonals. For three or more points, it must also compare different orders of combining the insertions.

    For the associative word construction, a configuration is an ordered list of positions. The lists (x,y)(x,y) and (x,y,x)(x,y,x), with x≠yx\ne y, are distinct word configurations even though they occupy the same two points. Coefficient complexes have coherent derived-pullback identifications when consecutive positions collide. Their convolution combines consecutive blocks on the open set where the two blocks are disjoint. Factorization is a condition on the bar coalgebra: its cut coproduct identifies the coefficient on that open set with the external product of the two block coefficients. The ordered collision atlas gives a second coefficient category, with a different convolution. Chapters 4–5 specify both constructions.

    1.3 Why representations and centres enter

    A local algebra is also tested by the objects on which it acts. An ordinary representation of an algebra AA is a vector space MM with an action A⊗M→MA\otimes M\to M. In the field-theoretic setting, boundary conditions and line operators lead to corresponding module constructions. Combining two such objects requires more than knowing the action on each separately.

    For an ordinary bialgebra HH, a coproduct Δ:H→H⊗H\Delta:H\to H\otimes H supplies the diagonal action on M⊗NM\otimes N:

    h⋅(m⊗n)=∑h(1)m⊗h(2)n,Δ(h)=∑h(1)⊗h(2).h\cdot(m\otimes n) =\sum h_{(1)}m\otimes h_{(2)}n, \qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.
    (1.6)

    The compatibility between multiplication and coproduct makes this an action. Coassociativity controls its associativity on three modules. Maps interchanging the factors require additional structure: cocommutativity supplies the usual flip, while a more general exchange requires a braiding and its compatibility equations. A chiral quantum group must solve the corresponding problem with local position-dependent operations.

    Centres arise from a different aspect of representation theory. A central element of AA acts on every AA-module and commutes with the action. When modules and their relations are represented by complexes, the analogous compatible operations include homotopies. A derived centre retains that higher information. This gives a precise possible target for a bulk-to-boundary comparison: bulk observables may act compatibly on the boundary's modules and interfaces.

    The existence of such an action does not by itself prove reconstruction. First one must construct the map from independently defined bulk observables and ask whether it recovers the observable algebra. A separate construction may give a functor F:𝒞bulk→𝒞∂F:\mathcal C_{\mathrm{bulk}}\to\mathcal C_{\partial} between categories of bulk and boundary modules. Full faithfulness is then a statement about that functor: it must identify the morphisms between every pair of modules, with the appropriate higher mapping data when these are present. An equivalence of the observable algebras and an equivalence of these module categories are distinct claims. Products, gluing and states impose further comparisons.

    1.4 The mathematical problem in its present form

    The theory already contains substantial examples of the required structures. There are ordinary module duality theorems on explicitly stated parameter ranges; local operations for every finite number of inputs on a common formal domain; theorems characterizing specified factorizing objects through their actions; analytic conformal-block compositions; and numerical Gaussian states on controlled field domains. Geometric Hall constructions, branes and arithmetic trace theories provide further realizations with their own coefficients and operations.

    Their limitations are informative because they distinguish the next comparisons. A theorem for every finite arity on one common Laurent-series space need not define an operation on separately completed intermediate spaces. A module duality at a generic parameter need not persist at a singular parameter. Agreement of traces need not identify a state algebra. A numerical state need not identify the state prepared by an independently specified geometric cap—a region with boundary, fields and boundary conditions whose path integral prepares that boundary state.

    The central question is therefore concrete: which algebraic and geometric operations can be transported between the independently defined constructions, on which objects, and with which normalizations? The answers may include equivalences, exact restrictions to a class of modules, or obstructions to a specified comparison. Each answer must retain the positive structures it explains.

    The Gaussian calculation gives the first criterion. A reduction must carry observables, their products and their normalization together. Locality adds positions and collision behaviour. Representation theory adds modules and the operation that combines them. The next chapter develops the ordinary algebraic maps that make these requirements precise; the subsequent chapters explain what changes when their inputs are local fields.

    Algebras, modules and combining systems

    The boundary reconstruction problem uses an algebra in two ways. Its product describes how observables compose. Its representations describe the systems on which those observables act. A quantum-group structure must also explain how to combine two representations. These requirements lead to different maps, and the distinction remains important when the maps become chiral.

    We begin over a field kk, usually ℂ\mathbb C, with ordinary ungraded vector spaces. All tensor products in this chapter are algebraic tensor products over kk. Completions and the signs for complexes will be introduced when they are needed.

    2.1 Multiplication and representations

    A unital associative algebra consists of a vector space AA, a bilinear multiplication m:A⊗A→Am:A\otimes A\to A, and an element 1A1_A such that

    (ab)c=a(bc),1Aa=a=a1A.(ab)c=a(bc),\qquad 1_Aa=a=a1_A.

    Equivalently, the unit is a linear map uA:k→Au_A:k\to A, uA(1)=1Au_A(1)=1_A. For an algebra of operators, associativity is the statement that three successive operations have a well-defined composite.

    A left AA-module is a vector space MM together with an action ρM:A⊗M→M\rho_M:A\otimes M\to M satisfying

    (ab)m=a(bm),1Am=m.(ab)m=a(bm),\qquad 1_Am=m.

    A map of modules f:M→Nf:M\to N is a linear map with f(am)=af(m)f(am)=af(m). Such a map compares the systems together with their observable actions, not merely their underlying vector spaces.

    For example, let A=k[x]A=k[x]. For every λ∈k\lambda\in k, there is a one-dimensional module kλk_\lambda on which xx acts by multiplication by λ\lambda. A module map f:kλ→kμf:k_\lambda\to k_\mu must satisfy

    λf(1)=μf(1).\lambda f(1)=\mu f(1).

    Thus kλk_\lambda and kμk_\mu are isomorphic precisely when λ=μ\lambda=\mu. Their dimensions agree for every pair of parameters. A counting invariant of the state space has discarded the action that distinguishes them.

    This is the first reason that reconstruction uses a category of modules. The category contains the objects, their action-preserving maps and the way those maps compose. A numerical character or partition function can be extracted from this information under suitable hypotheses, but it need not recover it.

    2.2 A coproduct gives the action on a tensor product

    Suppose MM and NN are representations of the same algebra HH. Their vector-space tensor product exists, but an HH-action on it has not yet been specified. If we have a linear map

    Δ:H⟶H⊗H,\Delta:H\longrightarrow H\otimes H,

    we can try

    h⋅(m⊗n)=∑h(1)m⊗h(2)n,Δ(h)=∑h(1)⊗h(2).h\cdot(m\otimes n) =\sum h_{(1)}m\otimes h_{(2)}n, \qquad \Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.
    (2.1)

    The notation on the right denotes a finite sum representing the algebraic tensor Δ(h)\Delta(h).

    For (2.1) to be a representation, multiplication must be respected:

    Δ(hh′)=Δ(h)Δ(h′),Δ(1H)=1H⊗1H.\Delta(hh')=\Delta(h)\Delta(h'),\qquad \Delta(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H.
    (2.2)

    For three modules, the two resulting actions agree under the usual vector-space associator if

    (Δ⊗id)Δ=(id⊗Δ)Δ.(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta =(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta.
    (2.3)

    This is coassociativity. It compares two maps from HH to H⊗3H^{\otimes3}.

    There is also a distinguished one-dimensional representation if we have an algebra map ϵ:H→k\epsilon:H\to k. It serves as the tensor unit when

    (ϵ⊗id)Δ=id=(id⊗ϵ)Δ.(\epsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta =\mathrm{id} =(\mathrm{id}\otimes\epsilon)\Delta.
    (2.4)

    The map ϵ\epsilon is the coalgebra counit. An algebra HH with Δ\Delta and ϵ\epsilon satisfying (2.2)–(2.4) is a bialgebra.

    The product–coproduct compatibility can be written as one equation between maps H⊗H→H⊗HH\otimes H\to H\otimes H:

    Δm=(m⊗m)(id⊗τ⊗id)(Δ⊗Δ),\Delta m =(m\otimes m) (\mathrm{id}\otimes\tau\otimes\mathrm{id}) (\Delta\otimes\Delta),
    (2.5)

    where τ(a⊗b)=b⊗a\tau(a\otimes b)=b\otimes a. The middle interchange places the first components together and the second components together. This equation is the ordinary model for one of the compatibility problems in a chiral quantum group. The chiral problem must specify the position-dependent operation spaces and their interchange before it can assert the corresponding equation.

    2.3 Group multiplication reverses direction on functions

    The coproduct has a direct geometric origin. For an affine algebraic group GG, write 𝒪(G)\mathcal O(G) for its algebra of regular functions. Group multiplication is a map

    μ:G×G⟶G.\mu:G\times G\longrightarrow G.

    Pullback of functions reverses its direction:

    μ∗:𝒪(G)⟶𝒪(G×G)=𝒪(G)⊗𝒪(G).\mu^*:\mathcal O(G)\longrightarrow \mathcal O(G\times G) =\mathcal O(G)\otimes\mathcal O(G).

    This is the coproduct. Associativity of μ\mu becomes coassociativity of μ∗\mu^*, and evaluation at the identity of GG becomes the counit.

    For the additive group, 𝒪(G)=k[x]\mathcal O(G)=k[x], and

    Δ(x)=x⊗1+1⊗x,ϵ(x)=0.\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x,\qquad \epsilon(x)=0.
    (2.6)

    It follows that

    Δ(x2)=x2⊗1+2x⊗x+1⊗x2.\Delta(x^2)=x^2\otimes1+2x\otimes x+1\otimes x^2.

    The mixed term is forced by compatibility with multiplication. Under (2.1), the tensor product of kλk_\lambda and kμk_\mu is kλ+μk_{\lambda+\mu}. The action, tensor product and group law now express the same operation in three forms.

    This passage from geometric maps to maps of observables is a basic source of quantum-group structures. Its tensor product must be interpreted in the category at hand: the equality above is an algebraic statement for affine schemes. It is not a license to replace a required completed tensor product of smooth or analytic functions by an algebraic tensor product. Drinfeld develops this viewpoint in Quantum groups, §1.

    2.4 Lie algebra actions and dual representations

    Let 𝔤\mathfrak g be a Lie algebra. Its universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤)U(\mathfrak g) is generated by 𝔤\mathfrak g with relations

    xy−yx=[x,y].xy-yx=[x,y].

    The primitive formula

    Δ(x)=x⊗1+1⊗x(x∈𝔤)\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x \qquad(x\in\mathfrak g)
    (2.7)

    extends to a coproduct on U(𝔤)U(\mathfrak g). To see why the relations survive, calculate

    [Δ(x),Δ(y)]=[x,y]⊗1+1⊗[x,y]=Δ([x,y]).[\Delta(x),\Delta(y)] =[x,y]\otimes1+1\otimes[x,y] =\Delta([x,y]).

    The cross commutators vanish because the two tensor factors commute. Formula (2.1) becomes the familiar diagonal Lie algebra action

    x(m⊗n)=(xm)⊗n+m⊗(xn).x(m\otimes n)=(xm)\otimes n+m\otimes(xn).

    Dual representations require a reversal as well. On the algebraic dual M∨=Homk⁡(M,k)M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_k(M,k), the Lie action is

    (xϕ)(m)=−ϕ(xm).(x\phi)(m)=-\phi(xm).
    (2.8)

    The minus sign makes the evaluation pairing invariant:

    (xϕ)(m)+ϕ(xm)=0.(x\phi)(m)+\phi(xm)=0.

    For the enveloping algebra, this is expressed using the antipode SS, defined by S(x)=−xS(x)=-x and S(ab)=S(b)S(a)S(ab)=S(b)S(a). The order reversal is necessary because transposing a product reverses the order of the operators.

    In finite dimension, duality also gives the usual coevaluation map k→M⊗M∨k\to M\otimes M^\vee. In infinite dimension the formal expression ∑imi⊗mi∨\sum_i m_i\otimes m_i^\vee need not be an algebraic tensor. Evaluation, coevaluation and biduality therefore have different domain requirements. This distinction will recur when line operators and completed state spaces are compared.

    2.5 Associators, exchange and coherence

    Even when tensor products are associative up to canonical isomorphism, the isomorphisms must agree with one another. For three objects there is an associator

    αL,M,N:(L⊗M)⊗N⟶L⊗(M⊗N).\alpha_{L,M,N}:(L\otimes M)\otimes N \longrightarrow L\otimes(M\otimes N).

    For four objects, the pentagon identity says that the two paths from

    ((L⊗M)⊗N)⊗PtoL⊗(M⊗(N⊗P))((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes P \quad\text{to}\quad L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes P))

    agree. One path uses two associators; the other uses three. This is an equation of maps, not merely an assertion that the initial and final objects are isomorphic.

    A braiding is a natural family of isomorphisms

    βM,N:M⊗N⟶N⊗M,\beta_{M,N}:M\otimes N\longrightarrow N\otimes M,

    compatible with maps of both input objects. It has its own compatibility with composition. With parentheses identified by the associator, its two hexagon equations read

    βL,M⊗N=(idM⊗βL,N)(βL,M⊗idN),\beta_{L,M\otimes N} =(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\beta_{L,N}) (\beta_{L,M}\otimes\mathrm{id}_N),
    (2.9)
    βL⊗M,N=(βL,N⊗idM)(idL⊗βM,N).\beta_{L\otimes M,N} =(\beta_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M) (\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\beta_{M,N}).
    (2.10)

    These equations say that moving one object past a pair agrees with moving it past the two factors successively.

    For ordinary vector spaces, the flip provides such a braiding. For HH-modules it is action-preserving when the coproduct is cocommutative, meaning τΔ=Δ\tau\Delta=\Delta. A noncocommutative coproduct requires additional data to obtain an exchange map. In local field theories, the exchange can also depend on positions and continuation paths. The associator and hexagon equations then become part of the comparison to be proved.

    Here coherence means these specified compatibility equations. For complexes, some equalities are replaced by homotopies, which must satisfy further equations of their own. Retaining an associator without its pentagon, or a binary homotopy without the next compatibility, retains only part of the structure.

    2.6 Universal maps and the other meaning of counit

    There is another common source of units and counits that does not require a coproduct. Let F(V)=A⊗VF(V)=A\otimes V be the free left AA-module on a vector space VV, and let U(M)U(M) denote the underlying vector space of an AA-module. A linear map g:V→U(M)g:V\to U(M) extends uniquely to

    g~:A⊗V⟶M,g~(a⊗v)=ag(v).\widetilde g:A\otimes V\longrightarrow M, \qquad \widetilde g(a\otimes v)=ag(v).

    Conversely, an AA-linear map g~\widetilde g is determined by its values on 1A⊗V1_A\otimes V. Thus

    HomA⁡(FV,M)≅Homk⁡(V,UM).\operatorname{Hom}_A(FV,M) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,UM).
    (2.11)

    This natural bijection is an adjunction F⊣UF\dashv U.

    Its unit is the natural map

    ηV:V⟶UFV,v⟼1A⊗v,\eta_V:V\longrightarrow UFV,\qquad v\longmapsto1_A\otimes v,

    and its counit is

    εM:FUM⟶M,a⊗m⟼am.\varepsilon_M:FUM\longrightarrow M,\qquad a\otimes m\longmapsto am.
    (2.12)

    The first triangle identity sends a⊗va\otimes v to a⊗1A⊗va\otimes1_A\otimes v and then back to a⊗va\otimes v. The second sends mm to 1A⊗m1_A\otimes m and then to mm. These identities express the compatibility of the free construction with evaluation.

    The adjunction counit εM:A⊗M→M\varepsilon_M:A\otimes M\to M is not the coalgebra counit ϵ:H→k\epsilon:H\to k. The former is part of a comparison between categories; the latter is part of a coalgebra. Neither by itself specifies a numerical quantum state. Later duality statements concern the unit and counit of particular derived adjunctions, and their invertibility must be proved.

    The ordinary maps are now explicit: multiplication composes observables, coproduct combines actions, associators and braidings compare different compositions, and an adjunction compares constructions by a universal property. Local fields require the same care, with the additional fact that every input has a position. The next chapter studies how the current singularity in (1.4) modifies these operations.

    Part I Observables, representations and localityChapter 3 of 18

    3

    Local fields on a curve

    An ordinary algebra assigns a product to two observables without recording where they are inserted. A boundary field theory needs the positions as well. The current in Chapter 1 already exhibits the new feature: its product contains a pole when the two insertion points meet. The pole has coefficients that are themselves fields. A local algebra must retain those coefficients, their action on states, and the rules for expanding a product in different regions.

    We begin on a complex coordinate disc. The constructions in this chapter are algebraic: a Laurent series is a formal series, and a field is an operator-valued formal distribution. Convergence of matrix coefficients on an analytic region is an additional assertion, developed in Chapter 10. This distinction lets us define the local operations before choosing a Hilbert space or an integration contour.

    3.1 Fields and their modes

    Let VV be a complex vector space of states. A field on VV is a series

    A(z)=∑n∈ℤAnz−n−1,An∈Endℂ⁡(V),A(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}A_nz^{-n-1}, \qquad A_n\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V),
    (3.1)

    such that, for each v∈Vv\in V, the vector AnvA_nv vanishes for all sufficiently large nn. The bound may depend on vv. Consequently A(z)vA(z)v belongs to V((z))V((z)): it has only finitely many negative powers of zz, although it may have infinitely many positive powers. The operators AnA_n are the modes of the field.

    The coefficient notation is arranged so that

    Anv=Resz=0⁡znA(z)vdz.A_n v=\operatorname{Res}_{z=0}z^n A(z)v\,dz.

    Here the formal residue extracts the coefficient of z−1z^{-1}. No analytic integral is required for this definition. If a particular matrix coefficient is represented by a convergent meromorphic function, the same coefficient is its usual contour residue.

    The products A(z)B(w)A(z)B(w) and B(w)A(z)B(w)A(z) initially have different expansion conventions. Their difference is interpreted as a two-variable formal distribution. Two fields are local if there is an integer N≥0N\geq0 such that

    (z−w)N[A(z),B(w)]=0.(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0.
    (3.2)

    We are using even, or bosonic, fields; fields with odd parity require the corresponding graded commutator. Equation (3.2) says that multiplying by a sufficiently high power of the collision equation removes the difference between the two expansions. It does not assign a finite product at z=wz=w.

    For example, write ιz,w\iota_{z,w} for expansion in nonnegative powers of w/zw/z, and ιw,z\iota_{w,z} for expansion in nonnegative powers of z/wz/w. Then

    ιz,w1(z−w)2=∑r≥0(r+1)wrz−r−2,ιw,z1(z−w)2=∑r≥0(r+1)zrw−r−2.\iota_{z,w}\frac1{(z-w)^2} =\sum_{r\geq0}(r+1)w^rz^{-r-2}, \qquad \iota_{w,z}\frac1{(z-w)^2} =\sum_{r\geq0}(r+1)z^rw^{-r-2}.
    (3.3)

    These are expansions of the same rational function in two different regions. As formal distributions they are different. Multiplication by (z−w)2(z-w)^2 makes both equal to 11, so it kills their difference. This is the mechanism behind the locality equation for the current below.

    3.2 A vertex algebra retains states and local products

    A vertex algebra packages a compatible family of fields on one state space. In the even convention used here, its data are a vector space VV, a vacuum vector 𝟏\mathbf1, a translation operator T:V→VT:V\to V, and a linear assignment

    a⟼Y(a,z)=∑n∈ℤa(n)z−n−1a\longmapsto Y(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{(n)}z^{-n-1}

    of a field to every state aa. They satisfy the vacuum and creation identities

    Y(𝟏,z)=idV⁡,Y(a,z)𝟏∈a+zV[[z]],Y(\mathbf1,z)=\operatorname{id}_V, \qquad Y(a,z)\mathbf1\in a+zV[[z]],
    (3.4)

    the translation identities

    T𝟏=0,[T,Y(a,z)]=∂zY(a,z)=Y(Ta,z),T\mathbf1=0, \qquad [T,Y(a,z)]=\partial_zY(a,z)=Y(Ta,z),
    (3.5)

    and locality for every pair Y(a,z),Y(b,w)Y(a,z),Y(b,w). These conditions express the state–field correspondence, the infinitesimal motion of an insertion, and the compatibility of products at distinct positions. They imply

    Y(a,z)𝟏=ezTa,a=a(−1)𝟏.Y(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a, \qquad a=a_{(-1)}\mathbf1.

    Thus the vacuum connects an operator-valued field with the state it creates. It has not yet supplied a scalar-valued vacuum expectation: that requires a linear functional or pairing in addition.

    The singular part of the product is written

    Y(a,z)Y(b,w)∼∑n≥0Y(a(n)b,w)(z−w)n+1.Y(a,z)Y(b,w) \sim\sum_{n\geq0} \frac{Y(a_{(n)}b,w)}{(z-w)^{n+1}}.
    (3.6)

    The symbol ∼\sim means equality of singular parts in the indicated expansion convention. The sum is finite for each pair of states. The regular coefficients also belong to the vertex-algebra structure: in particular, a(−1)ba_{(-1)}b defines the normally ordered product. Retaining only (3.6) therefore retains less information than the full state–field map.

    One can collect the singular coefficients into a polynomial in a formal variable λ\lambda:

    [aλb]=∑n≥0λnn!a(n)b.[a_\lambda b]=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}a_{(n)}b.
    (3.7)

    This λ\lambda-bracket is convenient for differential identities. It records the singular products; it is not, by itself, a definition of the full vertex algebra. Beilinson and Drinfeld relate vertex algebras to translation-equivariant chiral algebras on the affine line in Chiral Algebras, §0.15, and express the state–field operation geometrically in §3.5.

    3.3 The free current as a complete calculation

    Let κ∈ℂ\kappa\in\mathbb C. Consider operators JnJ_n, for n∈ℤn\in\mathbb Z, satisfying

    [Jm,Jn]=κmδm+n,0id⁡.[J_m,J_n]=\kappa m\,\delta_{m+n,0}\operatorname{id}.
    (3.8)

    Here δr,0\delta_{r,0} is 11 for r=0r=0 and 00 otherwise. A vacuum representation with zero charge is

    V=ℂ[x1,x2,x3,…],𝟏=1,V=\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots], \qquad \mathbf1=1,

    where

    J−n=xn⋅(−),Jn=κn∂∂xn(n>0),J0=0.J_{-n}=x_n\cdot(-),\qquad J_n=\kappa n\frac{\partial}{\partial x_n} \quad(n>0), \qquad J_0=0.
    (3.9)

    Every polynomial involves only finitely many variables, so JnJ_n annihilates it for all sufficiently large positive nn. Hence

    J(z)=∑n∈ℤJnz−n−1J(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}J_nz^{-n-1}

    is a field. The commutator in (3.8) follows directly from differentiation and multiplication. The negative modes create polynomial factors; the positive modes remove them.

    Split the field into

    J−(z)=∑n<0Jnz−n−1,J+(z)=∑n≥0Jnz−n−1.J_-(z)=\sum_{n<0}J_nz^{-n-1}, \qquad J_+(z)=\sum_{n\geq0}J_nz^{-n-1}.

    Normal ordering places the creation operators to the left:

    :J(z)J(w):=J−(z)J(w)+J(w)J+(z).:J(z)J(w):=J_-(z)J(w)+J(w)J_+(z).

    Commuting the remaining positive modes through J(w)J(w) gives

    J(z)J(w)=:J(z)J(w):+[J+(z),J(w)]=:J(z)J(w):+κ∑n≥1nz−n−1wn−1=:J(z)J(w):+κιz,w1(z−w)2.\begin{aligned} J(z)J(w) &=:J(z)J(w):+[J_+(z),J(w)]\\ &=:J(z)J(w):+ \kappa\sum_{n\geq1}n z^{-n-1}w^{n-1}\\ &=:J(z)J(w):+ \kappa\,\iota_{z,w}\frac1{(z-w)^2}. \end{aligned}
    (3.10)

    The double pole is the sum of the mode commutators. In state notation, if j=x1j=x_1, then j(1)j=κ𝟏j_{(1)}j=\kappa\mathbf1 and the other singular products vanish. Thus [jλj]=κλ𝟏[j_\lambda j]=\kappa\lambda\mathbf1.

    Define TT on the polynomial algebra as the derivation

    Txn=nxn+1.Tx_n=n x_{n+1}.

    It satisfies [T,Jn]=−nJn−1[T,J_n]=-nJ_{n-1}, hence [T,J(z)]=∂zJ(z)[T,J(z)]=\partial_zJ(z). The fields of polynomial states are generated by normal products and derivatives; for example,

    Y(x2,z)=∂zJ(z),Y(x12,z)=:J(z)2:.Y(x_2,z)=\partial_zJ(z), \qquad Y(x_1^2,z)=:J(z)^2:.

    This is the rank-one Heisenberg vertex algebra. The central coefficient κ\kappa is part of its structure. Choosing a positive real value may support further analytic constructions, but the algebraic construction above assumes no positivity.

    The functional ⟨𝟏∗,−⟩\langle\mathbf1^*,-\rangle that takes the constant term of a polynomial gives

    ⟨𝟏∗,J(z)J(w)𝟏⟩=κιz,w(z−w)−2.\langle\mathbf1^*,J(z)J(w)\mathbf1\rangle =\kappa\,\iota_{z,w}(z-w)^{-2}.
    (3.11)

    This particular two-point coefficient is the expansion of a meromorphic function. Its existence follows here from the explicit vacuum representation and functional. A different representation, charge or functional is additional data, even when the local mode relations remain the same.

    3.4 Nonabelian currents and the information in a pole

    Let 𝔤\mathfrak g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra with an invariant symmetric bilinear form (x,y)(x,y), and let ℓ∈ℂ\ell\in\mathbb C be a level. The affine current relations are

    [Jmx,Jny]=Jm+n[x,y]+ℓm(x,y)δm+n,0id⁡.[J^x_m,J^y_n] =J^{[x,y]}_{m+n} +\ell m(x,y)\delta_{m+n,0}\operatorname{id}.
    (3.12)

    Invariance means ([x,y],z)=(x,[y,z])([x,y],z)=(x,[y,z]); it is the compatibility required for the central term to satisfy the Jacobi identity. The associated current expansion is

    Jx(z)Jy(w)∼J[x,y](w)z−w+ℓ(x,y)(z−w)2.J^x(z)J^y(w) \sim\frac{J^{[x,y]}(w)}{z-w} +\frac{\ell(x,y)}{(z-w)^2}.
    (3.13)

    The simple pole records the Lie bracket, while the double pole records the central extension. Neither can be recovered from the dimension of the state space.

    For a direct check, take the zz-residue after multiplying the simple pole by zmz^m. It yields wmJ[x,y](w)w^mJ^{[x,y]}(w). The double pole yields the derivative mwm−1m w^{m-1}. Taking the ww-residue with wnw^n then gives precisely the two terms of (3.12). The residue calculation explains why a first derivative occurs in the central term.

    A module for the current algebra must specify the action of every mode. The local-field condition asks that sufficiently high positive modes kill each vector. This is a vectorwise condition, often called smoothness in this setting; it does not impose a single bound on the whole module. The induced vacuum modules and the derived functors studied in later chapters preserve this distinction. Their algebraic completions cannot be selected by the shape of an operator-product formula alone.

    3.5 Differentiation and a change of coordinates

    The coordinate zz made the mode calculation transparent. To move from a disc to a curve, one needs a way to differentiate sections and to compare their descriptions in different coordinates. The sheaf 𝒟X\mathcal D_X on a smooth curve XX is the sheaf of algebraic differential operators. On an affine coordinate chart its generators satisfy

    [∂z,z]=1.[\partial_z,z]=1.

    A left differential module, or left 𝒟X\mathcal D_X-module, is an 𝒪X\mathcal O_X-module MM with differentiation obeying the Leibniz rule

    ∇∂z(fm)=f′m+f∇∂zm.\nabla_{\partial_z}(fm)=f'm+f\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
    (3.14)

    For a vector bundle this is a connection. Differential modules may also be infinite-dimensional or supported on a subvariety, so they include more than vector bundles with connection.

    On the coordinate line, a vector space with an operator TT gives the example M=𝒪X⊗VM=\mathcal O_X\otimes V with

    ∇∂z(f⊗v)=f′⊗v+f⊗Tv.\nabla_{\partial_z}(f\otimes v)=f'\otimes v+f\otimes Tv.

    The equation records translation together with differentiation of scalar coefficients. It does not, on its own, give the response of a vertex algebra to every nonlinear coordinate change. To obtain a coordinate-independent construction on arbitrary curves, one supplies suitable coordinate-change actions; a conformal structure is a familiar way to obtain them. Translation-equivariant algebras on the affine line and coordinate-independent algebras on all curves are therefore different global assertions.

    Chiral operations are conventionally written for right differential modules. If MM is a left module, its corresponding right module is

    Mr=ωX⊗𝒪XM,M^{\mathrm r}=\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}M,

    where ωX\omega_X is the line bundle of one-forms. In a coordinate,

    (dz⊗m)⋅∂z=−dz⊗∇∂zm.(dz\otimes m)\cdot\partial_z=-dz\otimes\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
    (3.15)

    This conversion accounts for the signs and one-form factors in a geometric residue. It is an equivalence between left and right differential modules; it is not a duality of the state spaces.

    We now have the local ingredients: states, fields, mode actions, translation, and singular products. What remains is to put the operations on an actual space of several insertion points. The collision z=wz=w will become a diagonal subvariety, and the two expansion domains will become parts of a geometric gluing problem. That geometric formulation is the subject of Chapter 4.

    Part I Observables, representations and localityChapter 4 of 18

    4

    Factorization and collision geometry

    The free-current calculation has two descriptions. At distinct positions, two insertions give a product of fields. Near a collision, the same product is expressed through its singular and regular coefficients. A geometric algebra must say how these descriptions fit together, and how the answer behaves when three or more points approach one another.

    The coefficients of an associative chiral algebra are complexes on configurations and their collision strata. The permitted collisions and the convolution must be specified together. The word construction retains consecutive cuts; the full ordered collision atlas retains ordered decompositions into arbitrary subsets. We will compare their geometry with the classical Beilinson–Drinfeld operation spaces, then use it to define the associative objects and their bars.

    4.1 Configurations and partial diagonals

    Let XX be a smooth algebraic curve over a characteristic-zero field kk. For a finite nonempty set II, the product XIX^I records an II-labelled family of points. Its open configuration space is

    UI={(xi)∈XI:xi≠xj whenever i≠j}.U_I=\{(x_i)\in X^I:x_i\ne x_j\text{ whenever }i\ne j\}.
    (4.1)

    Write jI:UI↪XIj_I:U_I\hookrightarrow X^I for its inclusion. The small diagonal is the map

    ΔI:X⟶XI,x⟼(x)i∈I.\Delta_I:X\longrightarrow X^I, \qquad x\longmapsto(x)_{i\in I}.

    Its image is the locus where all the labelled points coincide. For two labels i,ji,j, the partial diagonal Δij\Delta_{ij} imposes only xi=xjx_i=x_j.

    A partition of the labels specifies which points are to be treated as one cluster. Represent it by a surjection π:J↠I\pi:J\twoheadrightarrow I, with blocks Ji=π−1(i)J_i=\pi^{-1}(i). Define

    Uπ={(xj)∈XJ:xj≠xj′ if π(j)≠π(j′)}.U_\pi=\{(x_j)\in X^J: x_j\ne x_{j'}\text{ if }\pi(j)\ne\pi(j')\}.
    (4.2)

    Points in different blocks must be distinct; points in the same block may collide. The associated diagonal map

    Δπ:XI⟶XJ,(xi)⟼(xπ(j))\Delta_\pi:X^I\longrightarrow X^J, \qquad(x_i)\longmapsto(x_{\pi(j)})

    inserts one repeated coordinate for every label in a block. Its image is the locus where the points in each block coincide.

    For J={1,2,3}J=\{1,2,3\} and blocks {1,2},{3}\{1,2\},\{3\}, the open set UπU_\pi permits x1=x2x_1=x_2, but excludes x1=x3x_1=x_3 and x2=x3x_2=x_3. It is the correct domain for first combining the first two insertions while keeping their cluster separate from the third. A second partition describes the other parenthesization. To compare the resulting operations, one must first put them in a common space of maps.

    4.2 A chiral operation is a map with a collision target

    Let LiL_i and MM be right 𝒟X\mathcal D_X-modules. Their external tensor product ⊠i∈ILi\boxtimes_{i\in I}L_i is a differential module on XIX^I: each factor depends on its own point. Allowing singularities along the collision diagonals gives

    jI∗jI∗(⊠i∈ILi).j_{I*}j_I^*\Bigl(\boxtimes_{i\in I}L_i\Bigr).

    For a divisor complement, this is the usual localization allowing poles along the omitted divisor. Locally, an individual section has a finite pole order; no single pole bound is imposed on the whole module. This algebraic localization is not a Laurent completion with an unspecified convergence condition.

    The direct image ΔI∗M\Delta_{I*}M is a differential module on XIX^I supported on the small diagonal. It includes derivatives in directions normal to that diagonal. A chiral II-operation is a differential-module map

    μ:jI∗jI∗(⊠i∈ILi)⟶ΔI∗M.\mu: j_{I*}j_I^*\Bigl(\boxtimes_{i\in I}L_i\Bigr) \longrightarrow\Delta_{I*}M.
    (4.3)

    Thus its space is

    PIch((Li);M)=Hom𝒟XI⁡(jI∗jI∗⊠iLi,ΔI∗M).P_I^{\mathrm{ch}}((L_i);M) =\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D_{X^I}} \left(j_{I*}j_I^*\boxtimes_iL_i,\Delta_{I*}M\right).
    (4.4)

    Both sides of the Hom belong to the same category on XIX^I. The source permits separated inputs and their poles; the target records an output concentrated at their collision. This is the operation space of Beilinson–Drinfeld, Chiral Algebras, §3.1.1.

    The simplest model is a residue. With a local normal coordinate t=z−wt=z-w, the functional associated to a pole of order rr acts on a test series f(t)f(t) by

    Rest=0⁡f(t)trdt=f(r−1)(0)(r−1)!.\operatorname{Res}_{t=0}\frac{f(t)}{t^r}\,dt =\frac{f^{(r-1)}(0)}{(r-1)!}.
    (4.5)

    A simple pole extracts a value; a double pole extracts a first derivative. Higher poles retain higher normal derivatives. The target in (4.3) is designed to hold this information. Substituting z=wz=w into a singular function would not define the operation.

    For three inputs, one can compose a binary operation on the first block with a second binary operation on its output and the remaining input. The partition open UπU_\pi keeps distinct clusters apart during the first step. Localization and the diagonal direct-image identities then place the composite in PJchP_J^{\mathrm{ch}}. These composition maps are associative. Beilinson–Drinfeld, §3.1.2, writes them for arbitrary surjections of finite sets; the geometry explains the intermediate domains that a bare expression such as μ(μ(a,b),c)\mu(\mu(a,b),c) suppresses.

    4.3 The Lie convention and the full operator product

    In the classical Beilinson–Drinfeld terminology, a nonunital chiral algebra is a right differential module AA with a binary operation

    μ∈P2ch(A,A;A)\mu\in P_2^{\mathrm{ch}}(A,A;A)

    satisfying skew-symmetry and the Jacobi identity in these operation spaces. It is a Lie algebra object for the chiral operations. A unit is a differential-module map ωX→A\omega_X\to A whose operation with AA is the canonical residue operation; see Chiral Algebras, §§3.3.1–3.3.3.

    The word “Lie” here does not mean that the theory has discarded the full operator product of Chapter 3. The chiral operation accepts sections with arbitrary allowed poles. After converting from right to left differential modules and taking the punctured formal neighbourhood of the diagonal, it determines an operator-product expansion with its regular as well as singular coefficients. In local coordinates this is a map of the form

    a⊠b⟼∑n∈ℤcn(w)(z−w)n,a\boxtimes b\longmapsto \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}c_n(w)(z-w)^n,
    (4.6)

    with a finite negative tail for fixed inputs and the specified differential-module interpretation of the coefficients.

    The compatibility is substantial. Beilinson–Drinfeld, Theorem 3.5.10, identifies their chiral Lie brackets with commutative and associative operator-product structures, where iterated products are required to lie in the appropriate common formal expansion space. Their commutativity is exchange of the point-labelled inputs; it does not say that all singular coefficients vanish. Their associativity includes the existence of the common target in which the two expansions can be compared. A family of unrelated Laurent formulas does not satisfy this condition merely because its first few coefficients agree.

    The comparison with our associative objects passes through a coalgebra. Apply chiral Chevalley chains to the Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral Lie algebra. Restrict the resulting collision diagram to monotone surjections, and project its coproduct to consecutive cuts. This gives a factorizing cut coalgebra. Its associative cobar is an associative chiral algebra of configuration complexes; Chapter 5 gives the definition. A comparison with the original fields and their vacuum is additional structure.

    The reverse construction requires an extension of the whole bar coalgebra to every finite-set surjection, with a compatible cocommutative coproduct and factorization on disjoint loci. Symmetry on distinct points alone does not supply those collision maps. Thus the classical Lie–commutative correspondence supplies a construction of associative word objects, rather than an identification of the two categories. Chapter 12 states the comparison with its chosen tensors.

    4.4 Factorization includes the collision extension

    A geometric product can instead be described by its values on finite configurations. At distinct points, independent insertions should combine as an external tensor product. As points collide, their combined object must specialize compatibly to the object attached to the resulting smaller configuration.

    In the classical algebraic formulation, a factorization algebra consists of quasi-coherent sheaves BIB_I on XIX^I, together with two kinds of identifications. A surjection π:J↠I\pi:J\twoheadrightarrow I gives the diagonal identification

    νπ:Δπ∗BJ→∼BI\nu_\pi:\Delta_\pi^*B_J\xrightarrow{\sim}B_I
    (4.7)

    and the factorization identification on the block-separation open

    cπ:⊠i∈IBJi|Uπ→∼BJ|Uπ.c_\pi: \left.\boxtimes_{i\in I}B_{J_i}\right|_{U_\pi} \xrightarrow{\sim} \left.B_J\right|_{U_\pi}.
    (4.8)

    The diagonal identifications compose under successive collapses. The factorization identifications compose under refinements of partitions, and these two systems agree when some clusters are collapsed while others remain separated. The sheaves have no nonzero local sections supported on the union of collision diagonals. A unit is a section 1∈B{1}1\in B_{\{1\}} whose external product with every local section extends across the two-point diagonal and restricts there to that section. These are the ordinary sheaf conditions of Chiral Algebras, §§3.4.2–3.4.4; in derived formulations the pullbacks, equivalences and compatibilities need their derived versions.

    For example, taking BI=𝒪XIB_I=\mathcal O_{X^I} gives the unit factorization algebra. The factorization maps are the evident identifications of functions in separate sets of variables; the unit is the constant function 11. More interesting examples retain nontrivial collision data even though their restrictions to pairwise-distinct points are external products.

    The full family is often described as a sheaf on the Ran space of XX. At the level of points, this is the set of finite nonempty subsets of XX; repeated labels specify the same subset. The maps Δπ\Delta_\pi express exactly those repetitions. One may use the compatible family (BI,νπ)(B_I,\nu_\pi) without treating the Ran space as an ordinary finite-dimensional variety.

    Theorem: classical factorization and chiral algebras. The above category of unital factorization algebras is equivalent to the category of unital Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras on XX. The factorization sheaves acquire a canonical differential-module structure, and the corresponding right differential module is ωX⊗B{1}\omega_X\otimes B_{\{1\}}.

    This is Chiral Algebras, Proposition 3.4.7 and Theorem 3.4.9. The forward construction uses factorization to compare sections away from diagonals and then applies the geometric residue operation to obtain (4.3). The inverse construction is controlled by a complex indexed by partitions and their diagonals: its differential combines the chiral operations, and its exactness makes the collision extensions compatible. This partition complex is the Chevalley–Cousin complex of §§3.4.10–3.4.12. The theorem is about the full compatible sheaf data, including collisions and the unit. Giving only (4.8) on a separated open set omits part of its hypothesis.

    4.5 The open locus cannot determine every extension

    The need for collision data can be seen before any elaborate example. Let D⊂YD\subset Y be a closed subvariety with complementary open inclusion j:U↪Yj:U\hookrightarrow Y. If KK is a nonzero sheaf or differential module supported on DD, then

    j∗K=0.j^*K=0.

    Consequently FF and F⊕︎KF\oplus K have the same restriction to UU. Observing the family only on the separated locus cannot distinguish them. This example does not assert that both objects satisfy the factorization-algebra axioms just stated: those axioms impose additional conditions precisely on such extensions. It shows why a separated identification requires an extension theorem before becoming a global identification.

    A morphism of sheaves may therefore become an isomorphism on UU while its kernel or cokernel remains nonzero on DD. Chapter 5 expresses the corresponding statement for complexes through sections supported on the collision locus.

    These elementary facts govern the later comparison of geometric centres, current operations and collision complexes. An equivalence on separated configurations remains a positive result. Its extension across a collision is another mathematical question, with a definite support where a discrepancy can live.

    4.6 Ordered points lead to a different support

    For the word construction, retain the external label order 1,…,n1,\ldots,n. This orders the inputs; it imposes no real order on points of the complex curve. A monotone surjection collapses consecutive labels, and the coefficient complexes carry coherent extraordinary-pullback identifications along its diagonal map. Only adjacent repetitions disappear from a word: (x,y,x)(x,y,x) with x≠yx\ne y retains the middle insertion. A consecutive cut after the pp-th input separates the blocks {1,…,p}\{1,\ldots,p\} and {p+1,…,n}\{p+1,\ldots,n\}. Its open set is

    Up,n−p={(xi):xi≠xj whenever i≤p<j}.U_{p,n-p}= \{(x_i):x_i\ne x_j\text{ whenever }i\leq p<j\}.
    (4.9)

    Collisions within either block are allowed. These are the opens used by the consecutive-cut tensor product in Chapter 5.

    At arity three there are only two cuts:

    U1,2=X3∖(Δ12∪Δ13),U2,1=X3∖(Δ13∪Δ23).U_{1,2}=X^3\setminus(\Delta_{12}\cup\Delta_{13}), \qquad U_{2,1}=X^3\setminus(\Delta_{13}\cup\Delta_{23}).

    Their common failure locus is

    Z3=X3∖(U1,2∪U2,1)=(Δ12∪Δ13)∩(Δ13∪Δ23)=Δ13.\begin{aligned} Z_3 &=X^3\setminus(U_{1,2}\cup U_{2,1})\\ &=(\Delta_{12}\cup\Delta_{13}) \cap(\Delta_{13}\cup\Delta_{23}) =\Delta_{13}. \end{aligned}
    (4.10)

    Indeed, if x1=x3x_1=x_3, both cuts have a coincident pair across the cut. Conversely, if both cuts fail and x1≠x3x_1\ne x_3, the first failure forces x1=x2x_1=x_2 and the second forces x2=x3x_2=x_3, a contradiction. Thus the first and third points can obstruct every consecutive cut while the second point lies elsewhere. The support is larger than the small diagonal.

    The full ordered collision atlas is constructed from one chart XIX^I for each total order on the labels. Two charts are glued where their orders agree within every set of coincident labels. The coefficient systems use extraordinary pullback along surjections with ordered fibres. Their convolution sums over all ordered decompositions I=A⊔BI=A\sqcup B, with the blocks separated. This convolution is symmetric monoidal, although an associative algebra for it may have noncommutative multiplication.

    Word convolution instead uses the initial and final intervals of one fixed order and is nonsymmetric. Restricting an atlas system to its increasing chart and projecting onto those consecutive decompositions gives the cut coproduct. The projection is generally not an equivalence: at two distinct points it can discard the reverse-order summand. Consequently the two convolutions, and the factorization conditions attached to them, remain distinct.

    The bar construction of Chapter 5 records multiplication and its higher associativity relations as a differential on words. At a configuration with nn labels, a product of more than nn positive factors vanishes. This finite arity bound gives the associative bar–cobar equivalence in each of the two coefficient categories, using its own convolution.

    Part II Duality and centresChapter 5 of 18

    5

    Bar constructions and coherent operations

    When three local fields are combined, there are two successive operations: combine the first two and then the third, or combine the last two and then the first. To compare them, fix a common configuration domain and a coefficient complex QQ in which both operations take values. They then give maps f,g:P→Qf,g:P\to Q, where PP is the complex of the three inputs. Constructing these maps into the same QQ is part of the problem. Their appropriate comparison can be a homotopy in the mapping complex Hom⁡(P,Q)\operatorname{Hom}(P,Q), rather than equality of formulas. With four fields, the comparisons must themselves satisfy a further homotopy relation.

    To describe this without hiding the compatibility conditions, we first work with ordinary vector spaces and algebras. The bar construction will organize multiplication, its relations and the relations between those relations. Only after that construction is explicit will we return to points moving on a curve.

    The reconstruction question is precise: can the operations on all ordered configurations be recovered from a coalgebra whose coproducts cut a configuration into consecutive blocks, including every higher homotopy? For coefficients equal to kk on the empty configuration, positive word length is bounded by the number of points. That finite bound permits a bar–cobar equivalence even for cohomologically unbounded coefficients. Its support theorem also explains why, for three ordered points, the collision of the first and third can matter without a collision with the second. Readers already familiar with dg algebras can begin with the word construction below; the first two sections fix conventions and give the elementary examples used to interpret it.

    5.1 Complexes retain the equations and their solutions

    A cochain complex is a sequence of vector spaces and linear maps

    ⋯⟶Vn−1→dVn→dVn+1⟶⋯,d2=0.\cdots\longrightarrow V^{n-1}\xrightarrow{d}V^n \xrightarrow{d}V^{n+1}\longrightarrow\cdots, \qquad d^2=0.

    The superscript is the cohomological degree, and the differential has degree +1+1. A vector killed by dd is a cycle; a vector of the form dwdw is a boundary. Their quotient is

    Hn(V)=ker⁡(d:Vn→Vn+1)/im⁡(d:Vn−1→Vn).H^n(V)=\ker(d:V^n\to V^{n+1})/ \operatorname{im}(d:V^{n-1}\to V^n).

    The distinction between a boundary and a chosen primitive matters. Knowing that v=dwv=dw is solvable does not specify ww, and different choices can enter later operations.

    Our shift convention is

    V[1]n=Vn+1,dV[1]=−dV.V[1]^n=V^{n+1},\qquad d_{V[1]}=-d_V.

    Thus a vector of degree rr in VV has degree r−1r-1 in V[1]V[1]. Write svsv for that shifted vector; ss has degree −1-1. Tensor products use the Koszul sign rule:

    d(v⊗w)=dv⊗w+(−1)|v|v⊗dw,d(v\otimes w)=dv\otimes w+(-1)^{|v|}v\otimes dw,

    where |v||v| denotes the degree of a homogeneous vector.

    A chain map f:V→Wf:V\to W commutes with the differentials. A homotopy from gg to ff is a degree-minus-one map hh satisfying

    f−g=dWh+hdV.f-g=d_Wh+hd_V.

    Homotopic maps induce the same cohomology map, but the homotopy contains information that this induced map forgets. More generally, maps of all degrees form a complex

    Homr⁡(V,W)=∏nHom⁡(Vn,Wn+r),∂f=dWf−(−1)rfdV.\operatorname{Hom}^r(V,W)=\prod_n\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,W^{n+r}), \qquad \partial f=d_Wf-(-1)^rfd_V.

    Chain maps are its degree-zero cycles, and homotopies identify maps whose difference is a boundary. The product over nn is intentional: a degree-rr map has a component on every degree of VV.

    A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if it induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. The ordinary derived category formally makes these maps invertible. We will also retain the derived mapping complexes, obtained by resolving the inputs as necessary, rather than keeping only their degree-zero cohomology. This enhanced form of the derived category remembers homotopies and homotopies between them; it is the meaning intended when the geometric theorem below refers to higher mapping spaces.

    Consider the complex

    ℂu1⊕︎ℂu2→ dt ℂv1⊕︎ℂv2,dtu1=tv1,dtu2=0,\mathbb C u_1\oplus\mathbb C u_2 \xrightarrow{\ d_t\ } \mathbb C v_1\oplus\mathbb C v_2, \qquad d_tu_1=tv_1,\quad d_tu_2=0,

    in degrees zero and one. For t≠0t\ne0, the u1,v1u_1,v_1 summand is contractible: set h(v1)=t−1u1h(v_1)=t^{-1}u_1 and let hh vanish on the other basis vectors. If pp projects to the remaining u2,v2u_2,v_2 summand and ii includes it, then

    dh+hd=1−ip.dh+hd=1-ip.

    Both cohomology groups have dimension one. At t=0t=0, both have dimension two. The Euler characteristic is zero throughout, but the contracting homotopy has a pole at the point where the cohomology changes. A fibrewise calculation and a comparison valid over the whole parameter line are therefore different assertions.

    5.2 Relations can leave a higher operation

    A differential graded algebra is a graded associative algebra AA, equipped with a differential satisfying

    d(ab)=(da)b+(−1)|a|adb.d(ab)=(da)b+(-1)^{|a|}a\,db.

    Its cohomology is an associative graded algebra. Passing to cohomology nevertheless loses information about how products become boundaries.

    Here is an explicit example. Let

    A=T(a,b,c,x,y),|a|=|b|=|c|=|x|=|y|=1,A=T(a,b,c,x,y),\qquad |a|=|b|=|c|=|x|=|y|=1,

    be the free associative graded algebra on five generators, with

    da=db=dc=0,dx=ab,dy=bc.da=db=dc=0,\qquad dx=ab,\qquad dy=bc.

    Extend dd by the graded Leibniz rule. Since a,b,ca,b,c are closed, d2=0d^2=0. The cohomology products [a][b][a][b] and [b][c][b][c] vanish. The chosen primitives x,yx,y then give

    z=ay+xc,dz=−abc+abc=0.z=ay+xc, \qquad dz=-abc+abc=0.

    This cycle is not a boundary: the degree-two boundaries are spanned by abab and bcbc, whereas ay+xcay+xc is a different linear combination of words in the free algebra.

    Changing xx or yy by a degree-one cycle changes [z][z] by an element of [a]H1(A)+H1(A)[c][a]H^1(A)+H^1(A)[c]. In this example H1(A)H^1(A) is spanned by [a],[b],[c][a],[b],[c], and that indeterminacy cannot remove the words ayay and xcxc. The resulting nonzero coset is a triple Massey product: a higher operation defined from two vanishing products and choices of their primitives. The multiplication table on cohomology records the two zero products but does not determine this further class.

    The same issue arises when an associative multiplication is transferred to a smaller complex. Suppose maps i:H→Ai:H\to A, p:A→Hp:A\to H and a homotopy hh satisfy pi=1pi=1 and dh+hd=1−ipdh+hd=1-ip. Projecting the product gives pμ(i⊗i)p\mu(i\otimes i) on HH. Composing products introduces the intermediate projection ipip; replacing it by the identity produces terms containing hh. Those terms are the first higher operations. A comparison that retains only the projected binary product can discard the very primitives needed to compose it.

    5.3 Words and the reduced bar construction

    An augmentation of a unital dg algebra is a dg algebra map ϵ:A→k\epsilon:A\to k, where kk is the ground field. It splits the underlying complex as A=k⋅1⊕︎A‾A=k\cdot1\oplus\bar A, with A‾=ker⁡ϵ\bar A=\ker\epsilon. The reduced bar construction, including its empty word, is

    BA=Tc(A‾[1])=k⊕︎⨁n≥1(A‾[1])⊗n.BA=T^c(\bar A[1]) =k\oplus\bigoplus_{n\ge1}(\bar A[1])^{\otimes n}.

    We write

    [a1|⋯|an]=sa1⊗⋯⊗san,|[a1|⋯|an]|=∑i|ai|−n.[a_1|\cdots|a_n]=sa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes sa_n, \qquad |[a_1|\cdots|a_n]|=\sum_i|a_i|-n.

    The superscript cc indicates the tensor coalgebra. Its coproduct splits a word at every position:

    Δ[a1|⋯|an]=∑i=0n[a1|⋯|ai]⊗[ai+1|⋯|an].\Delta[a_1|\cdots|a_n] =\sum_{i=0}^n[a_1|\cdots|a_i] \otimes[a_{i+1}|\cdots|a_n].

    The empty word is 11. This deconcatenation is coassociative because splitting at two positions gives the same three consecutive subwords in either order.

    The bar differential has two kinds of terms. It applies the differential of AA to one letter, or multiplies two adjacent letters. With our cohomological suspension convention, its defining components are

    b1(sa)=−s(da),b2(sa⊗sb)=(−1)|a|s(ab).b_1(sa)=-s(da),\qquad b_2(sa\otimes sb)=(-1)^{|a|}s(ab).

    They extend to words by applying the operation in each possible position. Passing a degree-one operation across a prefix contributes the degree of that prefix. Explicitly,

    b[a1|⋯|an]=∑i=1n(−1)1+∑j<i(|aj|−1)[a1|⋯|dai|⋯|an]+∑i=1n−1(−1)|ai|+∑j<i(|aj|−1)[a1|⋯|aiai+1|⋯|an].\begin{aligned} b[a_1|\cdots|a_n] ={}&\sum_{i=1}^n (-1)^{1+\sum_{j<i}(|a_j|-1)} [a_1|\cdots|da_i|\cdots|a_n]\\ &+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} (-1)^{|a_i|+\sum_{j<i}(|a_j|-1)} [a_1|\cdots|a_ia_{i+1}|\cdots|a_n]. \end{aligned}

    The equation b2=0b^2=0 expresses three familiar facts: d2=0d^2=0, the Leibniz rule, and associativity. For an ordinary algebra concentrated in degree zero, the internal-differential terms vanish, and

    b[a|b]=[ab],b[a|b|c]=[ab|c]−[a|bc].b[a|b]=[ab],\qquad b[a|b|c]=[ab|c]-[a|bc].

    Applying bb again gives [(ab)c]−[a(bc)]=0[(ab)c]-[a(bc)]=0. The length-three word makes the relation between the two multiplications into an explicit boundary equation. Longer words organize the compatible ways of repeating this operation. These are the usual algebraic bar formulas, expressed in cohomological degrees; see Loday–Vallette, Algebraic Operads, §§2.2–2.3.

    Two small algebras show what this complex measures. For A=k[x]A=k[x], augmented by x↦0x\mapsto0, the two-term free resolution

    0⟶A→xA⟶k⟶00\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow{\,x\,}A\longrightarrow k\longrightarrow0

    computes the same groups as the bar resolution. Tensoring over AA with kk kills its differential, so

    H∗(BA)=k⊕︎k⋅[x],|[x]|=−1.H^*(BA)=k\oplus k\cdot[x],\qquad |[x]|=-1.

    In the bar complex itself, [x2]=b[x|x][x^2]=b[x|x], and similarly higher powers in a single letter do not give new degree-minus-one classes.

    For A=k[ϵ]/(ϵ2)A=k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2), the augmentation ideal is one-dimensional and its product is zero. Every bar differential is therefore zero:

    BA=⨁n≥0k[ϵ|⋯|ϵ],H−n(BA)=k(n≥0).BA=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}k[\epsilon|\cdots|\epsilon], \qquad H^{-n}(BA)=k\quad(n\ge0).

    The corresponding free resolution has multiplication by ϵ\epsilon at every step. It is exact before tensoring with kk, and every differential becomes zero afterwards. Thus the single relation ϵ2=0\epsilon^2=0 produces homological information in arbitrarily long words. These groups are traditionally denoted TornA⁡(k,k)\operatorname{Tor}_n^A(k,k), with n=−cohomological degreen=-\text{cohomological degree}.

    5.4 One differential encodes all associativity homotopies

    The word complex also accommodates multiplication that is associative only through specified homotopies. A degree-one map bb on Tc(V[1])T^c(V[1]) is a coderivation if

    Δb=(b⊗1+1⊗b)Δ,\Delta b=(b\otimes1+1\otimes b)\Delta,

    with the graded tensor convention. Such a map is determined by its components

    bn:(V[1])⊗n⟶V[1].b_n:(V[1])^{\otimes n}\longrightarrow V[1].

    On a finite word only finitely many components can act. An uncurved A∞A_\infty-algebra structure is a coderivation with no constant component and with b2=0b^2=0. Undoing the shifts gives operations mn:V⊗n→Vm_n:V^{\otimes n}\to V of degree 2−n2-n. The suspended formulation fixes the signs without a separate convention for every arity.

    The length-one equation is m12=0m_1^2=0; length two says that m2m_2 is a chain map. At length three, the associator of m2m_2 is the boundary of a degree-minus-one operation. At length four, the homotopies along the five parenthesizations of a fourfold product form a closed compatibility expression, and the next operation supplies its primitive. Continuing gives all the equations at once. Equivalently, their suspended form is

    ∑r+s+t=nbr+1+t(1⊗r⊗bs⊗1⊗t)=0,\sum_{r+s+t=n} b_{r+1+t}(1^{\otimes r}\otimes b_s\otimes1^{\otimes t})=0,

    where composition of graded tensor maps supplies the signs.

    This is the meaning of coherence here: the actual operations and these compatibility equations are included in the structure. An associative product on cohomology does not provide them. Nor do a binary operation and one ternary homotopy determine all higher operations. The bar complex provides a place to write the entire family, while finite words ensure that its differential is an actual algebraic operation.

    5.5 Cobar reverses the construction

    Let C=k⊕︎C‾C=k\oplus\bar C be a coaugmented dg coalgebra. Its reduced coproduct is Δ‾:C‾→C‾⊗C‾\bar\Delta:\bar C\to\bar C\otimes\bar C, obtained by removing the two terms involving 11. The coalgebra is conilpotent if sufficiently many iterated reduced coproducts kill each element. The tensor coalgebra above has this property because a word cannot be split into more nonempty pieces than its length.

    The cobar construction is the tensor algebra

    ΩC=T(C‾[−1]).\Omega C=T(\bar C[-1]).

    Write ucuc for a generator in C‾[−1]\bar C[-1], so |uc|=|c|+1|uc|=|c|+1. If Δ‾c=∑c′⊗c′′\bar\Delta c=\sum c'\otimes c'', its differential is the derivation determined by

    dΩ(uc)=−u(dCc)+∑(−1)|c′|+1(uc′)(uc′′).d_\Omega(uc)=-u(d_Cc) +\sum(-1)^{|c'|+1}(uc')(uc'').

    Thus bar shortens words by multiplication, while cobar lengthens them by coproduct. The signs are compatible: when a,ba,b have degree zero, the generator u[a|b]u[a|b] in ΩBA\Omega BA satisfies

    dΩu[a|b]=−u[ab]+(u[a])(u[b]).d_\Omega u[a|b]=-u[ab]+(u[a])(u[b]).

    The map ΩBA→A\Omega BA\to A sending u[a]u[a] to aa and the longer single generators to zero respects this equation. Its extra generators explicitly encode the multiplication relations in AA.

    More generally, a degree-one map τ:C→A\tau:C\to A, vanishing on the coaugmentation and landing in A‾\bar A, is a twisting cochain when

    dAτ+τdC+μA(τ⊗τ)Δ‾=0.d_A\tau+\tau d_C+\mu_A(\tau\otimes\tau)\bar\Delta=0.

    Here (τ⊗τ)(c′⊗c′′)=(−1)|c′|τ(c′)⊗τ(c′′)(\tau\otimes\tau)(c'\otimes c'')=(-1)^{|c'|}\tau(c')\otimes\tau(c''). This one equation says exactly that uc↦τ(c)uc\mapsto\tau(c) extends to a dg algebra map ΩC→A\Omega C\to A. For conilpotent CC, iterating its reduced coproduct gives the corresponding dg coalgebra map C→BAC\to BA. We obtain the strict bar–cobar adjunction

    HomdgAlg⁡(ΩC,A)≅Tw⁡(C,A)≅HomdgCoalg⁡(C,BA).\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgAlg}(\Omega C,A) \cong\operatorname{Tw}(C,A) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgCoalg}(C,BA).

    An adjunction provides comparison maps. Whether those maps are equivalences requires a theorem about the objects and weak equivalences under consideration. The geometry of ordered configurations supplies an especially useful finiteness condition for such a theorem.

    5.6 Ordered cuts give a finite geometric bar construction

    Let XX be a smooth separated finite-type curve over a characteristic-zero field kk. Write 𝒟(Xn)\mathcal D(X^n) for the unbounded derived category of right algebraic differential modules with quasi-coherent underlying modules, retaining its higher mapping spaces. A word coefficient system consists of complexes Mn∈𝒟(Xn)M_n\in\mathcal D(X^n) for n≥1n\ge1, together with coherent equivalences

    dα!Mn≃Mm(α:[n]↠[m] monotone),d_\alpha^!M_n\simeq M_m \qquad \bigl(\alpha:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[m]\text{ monotone}\bigr),

    where dα(x)i=xα(i)d_\alpha(x)_i=x_{\alpha(i)}. Here dα!d_\alpha^! is extraordinary derived pullback. The equivalences include their compatibilities under composition and all higher homotopies. Add an isolated empty coefficient M0∈D(k)M_0\in D(k), with no collision arrow from a nonempty configuration to it. Denote this category by 𝒲X\mathcal W_X; the integer nn is the arity.

    For p+q=np+q=n, let Up,q⊂XnU_{p,q}\subset X^n be the open set on which every point in the first block is distinct from every point in the second. There is no separation condition within either block. With jp,q:Up,q↪Xnj_{p,q}:U_{p,q}\hookrightarrow X^n, define consecutive-cut convolution by

    (M⋆N)n=⨁p+q=nRjp,q∗jp,q∗(Mp⊠𝐋Nq).(M\star N)_n= \bigoplus_{p+q=n}Rj_{p,q*}j_{p,q}^* (M_p\boxtimes^{\mathbf L}N_q).

    The symbol ⊠𝐋\boxtimes^{\mathbf L} means derived external tensor product. Open direct image allows the prescribed singular behaviour along the removed diagonals; it is not a choice of a finite pole bound. Empty blocks contribute their complexes over kk. Iterated products use consecutive blocks in their written order. Localizing at their interblock diagonals gives the common domain for every parenthesization.

    The unit is 𝟏=(k,0,0,…)\mathbf1=(k,0,0,\ldots). An augmented algebra is connected in arity if its augmentation identifies A0A_0 with kk; a counital coaugmented coalgebra has the analogous condition C0≃kC_0\simeq k. This says nothing about cohomological degrees. The positive-arity summands A‾,C‾\bar A,\bar C have the decisive property

    (M1⋆⋯⋆Mr)n=0if all M0i=0 and r>n.(M^1\star\cdots\star M^r)_n=0 \quad\text{if all }M^i_0=0\text{ and }r>n.

    Indeed, every nonzero term assigns at least one point to each of the rr factors.

    Theorem: connected consecutive-cut duality. In 𝒲X\mathcal W_X, bar and cobar for consecutive-cut convolution are inverse equivalences between connected augmented coherent associative algebras and connected counital coaugmented coherent coassociative coalgebras. The equivalence includes their full mapping spaces. It requires no cohomological boundedness or finite-dimensionality of coefficients.

    “Coherent” means that all higher associativity or coassociativity comparisons are retained, not just the equations visible on cohomology. One can compute the equivalence with strict dg representatives. Its proof uses the arity filtration: the normalized bar and cobar layers are

    A‾⋆r[r],C‾⋆r[−r].\bar A^{\star r}[r],\qquad \bar C^{\star r}[-r].

    In arity nn, they vanish for r>nr>n. Consequently the relevant constructions stabilize after finitely many normalized stages in each coefficient. No interchange of an arbitrary infinite tensor product with an inverse limit is needed. The underlying filtered associative duality is developed by Matsuoka, Koszul duality between EnE_n-algebras and coalgebras in a filtered category, Lemmas 4.13 and 4.17 (arXiv:1409.6943v4); intrinsic bar and cobar are treated in Lurie, Higher Algebra, §5.2.2.

    There are two adjunction conventions to distinguish. The strict twisting-cochain construction above has Ωdg⊣Bdg\Omega_{\rm dg}\dashv B_{\rm dg}. The intrinsic connected equivalence also has the adjunction B⊣ΩB\dashv\Omega, with maps A→ΩBAA\to\Omega BA and BΩC→CB\Omega C\to C. The comparison of the two presentations identifies their equivalences, not their oppositely directed canonical chain maps.

    5.7 The support remembers which cuts were allowed

    A coalgebra CC is factorizing across consecutive cuts if, on every Up,n−pU_{p,n-p}, its cut coproduct

    Cn|Up,n−p⟶(Cp⊠𝐋Cn−p)|Up,n−pC_n|_{U_{p,n-p}}\longrightarrow (C_p\boxtimes^{\mathbf L}C_{n-p})|_{U_{p,n-p}}

    is an equivalence. An associative chiral algebra in the word category is an augmented E1E_1-algebra AA for consecutive-cut convolution, with A0≃kA_0\simeq k, whose bar coalgebra BABA factorizes in this sense. Here E1E_1 means that the multiplication and all its associativity homotopies are retained. Its augmentation ideal has zero empty coefficient. The support theorem below identifies these algebras by the support of their positive-arity coefficients. Put

    Zn=Xn∖⋃p=1n−1Up,n−p,Z1=X.Z_n=X^n\setminus\bigcup_{p=1}^{n-1}U_{p,n-p}, \qquad Z_1=X.

    For a complex FF, derived sections supported on ZZ, denoted RΓZFR\Gamma_ZF, form the fibre of the restriction map F→Rj∗j∗FF\to Rj_*j^*F to the complementary open set.

    Support theorem. Consecutive-cut duality restricts to an equivalence between factorizing coalgebras and connected algebras whose positive-arity coefficients vanish on every cut open. For a factorizing coalgebra,

    ΩCn≃RΓZn(Cn)[−1].\overline{\Omega C}_n\simeq R\Gamma_{Z_n}(C_n)[-1].

    The shift is part of the formula. To see its origin, index a cube by subsets of the n−1n-1 possible cuts. A subset of size r−1r-1 gives rr blocks, hence a cobar term shifted by [−r][-r]. The corresponding localization cube has shift [−(r−1)][-(r-1)]; the two totalizations differ by [−1][-1]. Factorization identifies the entire cut cube with the localization cube, including its maps.

    For three points,

    Z3=(Δ12∪Δ13)∩(Δ13∪Δ23)=Δ13.Z_3=(\Delta_{12}\cup\Delta_{13}) \cap(\Delta_{13}\cup\Delta_{23})=\Delta_{13}.

    Here Δij\Delta_{ij} is the diagonal xi=xjx_i=x_j. A configuration with x1=x3x_1=x_3 and x2x_2 elsewhere defeats both consecutive cuts. The support is therefore larger than the small diagonal where all three points coincide.

    The supported complex alone does not specify the associative algebra. The multiplication on the cut cobar also uses the inverse factorization maps on the separating opens. Its unit lies at the empty configuration. A vacuum marking is separate singleton data: an identification A{1}≅ωX⊗𝒪XGA_{\{1\}}\cong\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}G with a left differential module GG and a horizontal map 𝒪X→G\mathcal O_X\to G. A vacuum framing further compares the configuration operations with the simultaneous field products, preserving substitutions, translation and the vacuum.

    The same definition of an associative chiral algebra can be used with the symmetric convolution on the full ordered collision atlas. There, factorization requires each specified coproduct component to be an equivalence. Its support consequence differs from the cut theorem. If C=BAC=BA and UU is the two-point distinct locus, put V=(C{1}⊠C{1})|UV=(C_{\{1\}}\boxtimes C_{\{1\}})|_U. Componentwise factorization gives

    A{1,2}|U≃V[−2].\overline A_{\{1,2\}}|_U\simeq V[-2].

    Thus nonzero VV gives a nonzero coefficient away from the diagonal. Small-diagonal support on the atlas is instead characterized by a joint word-factorization condition, which compares the full direct sum of ordered word terms. It cannot be substituted for the componentwise condition defining the factorizing bar.

    We have obtained an equivalence of specified algebraic structures, with their homotopies and geometric supports. To turn it into a duality of representations, one must determine the functors on modules and inspect their unit and counit. Those maps, rather than a resemblance between two algebras, are the subject of the next chapter.

    Part II Duality and centresChapter 6 of 18

    6

    Derived adjunctions and induction

    A representation can be studied through the maps into it from a chosen module WW. These maps carry an action of the endomorphisms of WW, and tensoring them back with WW gives a candidate reconstruction. The question is whether

    W⊗B𝐋RHom⁡(W,M)⟶MW\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}\operatorname{RHom}(W,M)\longrightarrow M

    recovers the original representation, where BB is the appropriate derived endomorphism algebra with its opposite multiplication. The arrow matters: an isomorphism between the two objects would not by itself identify this reconstruction map.

    For affine current algebras, the useful WW has an entire horizontal regular representation at its lowest energy. Its endomorphisms lead to a differential graded algebra with even current generators and odd generators recording relations. We will obtain a conditional reconstruction theorem for every ordinary unbounded module over this algebra in the nonrational 𝔰𝔩3\mathfrak{sl}_3 case. The mechanism is finite: four successive derived augmentation factors vanish. At other levels, explicit infinite extensions show why the same conclusion can fail.
