    8.1 Tensor completion and matrix rank

    Consider the vector space V=ℂℕV=\mathbb C^{\mathbb N} of all complex sequences. The natural map

    V⊗ℂV⟶ℂℕ×ℕ,f⊗g⟼(figj)i,j≥0,V\otimes_{\mathbb C}V\longrightarrow \mathbb C^{\mathbb N\times\mathbb N}, \qquad f\otimes g\longmapsto(f_i g_j)_{i,j\geq0},

    has image the matrices of finite rank. A sum of rr elementary tensors has column space contained in the span of rr sequences; conversely, a finite-rank matrix can be expressed using a basis of its column space. The infinite identity matrix (δij)(\delta_{ij}) therefore does not belong to this image.

    Give the image the coordinatewise topology inherited from the full matrix space. Its completion is the full matrix space: finite-support matrices are dense, and the finite diagonal matrices converge coordinatewise to (δij)(\delta_{ij}). The identity matrix becomes available after this specified completion. Nothing in this calculation identifies the completion with a tensor product defined using a different topology.

    The same issue appears in the current constructions below, where matrix indices are replaced by cohomological degrees, bar lengths, current modes and Laurent exponents. We will keep these indices separate long enough to see which infinite expressions the operations can act on.

    8.2 Algebraic tensors and mapping complexes

    For cochain complexes M,NM,N, with differential of degree +1+1, the algebraic tensor complex has

    (M⊗N)n=⨁i+j=nMi⊗Nj,d(m⊗n)=dm⊗n+(−1)|m|m⊗dn.(M\otimes N)^n=\bigoplus_{i+j=n}M^i\otimes N^j, \qquad d(m\otimes n)=dm\otimes n+(-1)^{|m|}m\otimes dn.

    Every element has finite support along the cohomological diagonal. The mapping complex instead has

    Homr⁡(M,N)=∏iHom⁡(Mi,Ni+r),d(f)=dNf−(−1)rfdM.\operatorname{Hom}^{r}(M,N) =\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(M^i,N^{i+r}), \qquad d(f)=d_Nf-(-1)^rf d_M.

    A homogeneous map must specify a map on every input degree; the product records that requirement. If Mi=Ni=ℂM^i=N^i=\mathbb C for all integers ii, with zero differentials, then degree zero of the tensor complex contains a direct sum indexed by ℤ\mathbb Z, whereas degree zero of the mapping complex is a product indexed by ℤ\mathbb Z. Replacing either by the other changes the complex even in this elementary example.

    A topology makes a further distinction. Put the discrete topology on each copy of ℂ\mathbb C. Every continuous linear functional

    ∏i≥0ℂ⟶ℂ\prod_{i\geq0}\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb C

    depends on finitely many coordinates. Continuity makes its kernel contain a basic neighbourhood on which only finitely many coordinates are constrained. By contrast, an algebraic functional on ⨁iℂ\bigoplus_i\mathbb C can assign an arbitrary coefficient to every basis vector. Thus passing from a direct sum to a product and then taking a continuous dual can recover a direct sum. This conclusion depends on the displayed topology and on the discrete target.

    These examples explain why “take the dual” does not completely specify an operation for a field-theoretic construction. One must name the topology, the scalar ring and the degree totalization. The convention for shifts throughout this chapter is V[1]n=Vn+1V[1]^n=V^{n+1}.

    8.3 Laurent series with algebraic coefficients

    For a vector space VV over a field FF, define

    V((q))=⋃N∈ℤqNV[[q]].V((q))=\bigcup_{N\in\mathbb Z}q^N V[[q]].

    An element has one lower Laurent bound and an arbitrary sequence of coefficients in VV. If V=⨁j≥0FejV=\bigoplus_{j\geq0}Fe_j, then

    v(q)=∑j≥0qjejv(q)=\sum_{j\geq0}q^j e_j

    is allowed: each coefficient has finite support. There is no requirement that all coefficients lie in one finite-dimensional subspace of VV. Consequently

    V⊗FF((q))⊊V((q))V\otimes_F F((q))\subsetneq V((q))

    for this VV. A vector in the left side is a finite sum of Laurent series multiplied by fixed vectors of VV, so all its coefficients lie in one finite-dimensional subspace. The series v(q)v(q) does not.

    For a cochain complex, Laurent completion here means (V((q)))n=Vn((q))(V((q)))^n=V^n((q)), degree by degree. Its lower bound may depend on nn. If another product index is present, its lower bounds require a separate decision. For example, the family (q−r)r≥0(q^{-r})_{r\geq0} belongs to

    ∏r≥0F((q)),\prod_{r\geq0}F((q)),

    but not to (∏r≥0F)((q))(\prod_{r\geq0}F)((q)): the latter requires a lower bound common to all coordinates. In the current complex below, the product index includes exterior arity. Requiring one lower bound across every arity would discard valid cochains.

    There is also an order of scalar extension. Let

    A0=ℂ[λ,λ−1,(λ−1)−1],F=ℂ(λ).A_0=\mathbb C[\lambda,\lambda^{-1},(\lambda-1)^{-1}], \qquad F=\mathbb C(\lambda).

    The series ∑n≥2qn/(λ−n)\sum_{n\geq2}q^n/(\lambda-n) belongs to F[[q]]F[[q]]. It does not lie in A0[[q]]⊗A0FA_0[[q]]\otimes_{A_0}F. An element of this algebraic localization has a common denominator in A0A_0, whereas no one denominator clears the distinct poles λ=n\lambda=n. Scalar extension before completion therefore permits more series than algebraic localization afterwards.

    These distinctions also govern continuity. Multiplication by a fixed Laurent polynomial has a finite loss of qq-order. A family of operations is continuous on a completed direct sum only if the required bound applies before its support is allowed to grow. A bound depending on bar length, for instance, need not suffice when bar length grows with the Laurent exponent.

    8.4 The line algebra and its spectral tensor

    We now apply these conventions to a concrete comparison. Let

    𝔤=𝔰𝔩2(ℂ),κ(E,F)=1,κ(H,H)=2,k∈ℂ∖ℚ.\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C),\qquad \kappa(E,F)=1,\quad\kappa(H,H)=2,\qquad k\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Q.

    The affine mode algebra A=A−k−2A=A_{-k-2} has relations

    [xtr,yts]=[x,y]tr+s+rδr+s,0(−k−2)κ(x,y)1.[xt^r,yt^s]=[x,y]t^{r+s} +r\delta_{r+s,0}(-k-2)\kappa(x,y)1.

    Put 𝔫=t𝔤[t]\mathfrak n=t\mathfrak g[t], U=U(𝔤)U=U(\mathfrak g), and W=A⊗U(𝔫)ℂW=A\otimes_{U(\mathfrak n)}\mathbb C. A smooth affine module is one in which every vector is annihilated by all sufficiently high positive modes; the bound can depend on the vector.

    The differential graded line algebra Y=YkY=Y_k of Chapter 6 has even current generators BnaB_n^a and odd generators ca,nc_{a,n}, for n≥0n\geq0. The latter have cohomological degree one. Their internal energies are nn and n+1n+1, respectively; energy is a separate grading. To recall their concrete meaning, the induced Chevalley resolution

    P−p=A⊗Λp𝔫P^{-p}=A\otimes\Lambda^p\mathfrak n

    carries right operators Bna↦Rtat−n−atat−nB_n^a\mapsto R_{t_at^{-n}}-a_{t_at^{-n}} and ca,n↦ιa,n+1c_{a,n}\mapsto\iota_{a,n+1}. Here RR is right multiplication, axa_x is the exterior derivation obtained by projecting [x,−][x,-] to 𝔫\mathfrak n, and ιa,n+1\iota_{a,n+1} contracts the indicated positive mode. The differential of YY is compatible with these operators. They represent line operations on the boundary resolution, including the odd operations that would be lost by keeping only ordinary endomorphisms. The full presentation and its energy-restricted endomorphism comparison are given in Line operators and the boundary derived functor, §“Lifts of the line generators.”

    For ordinary, possibly unbounded, left YY-modules M,NM,N, form the algebraic tensor complex T=M⊗NT=M\otimes N. Let q=z−1q=z^{-1}. The spectral tensor has underlying complex T((q))T((q)), but its differential includes the interaction

    Sz(T)=(T((q)),dT+ρT(r(q))),S_z(T)=\bigl(T((q)),d_T+\rho_T(r(q))\bigr),
    r(q)=∑a,i,j≥0(−1)i(i+ji)qi+j+1(ca,i⊗Bja−Bia⊗ca,j).r(q)=\sum_{a,i,j\geq0}(-1)^i\binom{i+j}{i}q^{i+j+1} \bigl(c_{a,i}\otimes B_j^a-B_i^a\otimes c_{a,j}\bigr).

    The invariant form contracts the Lie indices. Every coefficient is a finite algebraic operator, and every term has positive qq-order. Write dYd_Y for the differential of YY. On the tensor-product algebra (Y⊗Y)((q))(Y\otimes Y)((q)), let QQ be the induced differential

    Q(a⊗b)=dYa⊗b+(−1)|a|a⊗dYb,Q(q)=0,Q(a\otimes b)=d_Ya\otimes b+(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes d_Yb, \qquad Q(q)=0,

    extended coefficientwise. The identity

    Qr+r2=0Q r+r^2=0

    makes the corrected differential square to zero. It is the equation that permits the interaction, rather than a prescription to tensor two representations and ignore their coupling.

    8.5 The incoming bar, its completion, and the outgoing bar

    The bar construction from Chapter 5 resolves the incoming module relations. Write 𝐁=Y⊗Y\mathbf B=Y\otimes Y. Its length-rr term is

    𝐁⊗𝐁⊗r⊗T,𝐁=𝐁/ℂ1,\mathbf B\otimes\overline{\mathbf B}^{\otimes r}\otimes T, \qquad\overline{\mathbf B}=\mathbf B/\mathbb C1,

    with total degree equal to internal cohomological degree minus rr. The relevant completed complex is

    ℬz(T)=(Tot⊕︎⁡Bar𝐁⁡(𝐁,T))((q)),d=dbar+Lr(q).\mathcal B_z(T)= \left(\operatorname{Tot}_{\oplus} \operatorname{Bar}_{\mathbf B}(\mathbf B,T)\right)((q)), \qquad d=d_{\rm bar}+L_{r(q)}.

    The tensor diagonals and bar lengths are summed before completion. At a fixed Laurent coefficient there are finitely many words and finitely many tensor-diagonal components. Those finite supports can grow with the exponent.

    The original augmentation ℬz(T)→Sz(T)\mathcal B_z(T)\to S_z(T) is a quasi-isomorphism. Its mechanism is instructive. Before the correction, insertion of a unit gives a contracting homotopy hh of Laurent order zero. Perturbing by δ=Lr(q)\delta=L_{r(q)} gives a homotopy of the form

    H=h(1+δh)−1=h∑j≥0(−δh)j.H=h(1+\delta h)^{-1} =h\sum_{j\geq0}(-\delta h)^j.

    Each occurrence of δ\delta raises qq-order. Only finitely many terms contribute to a fixed coefficient, and each such term is an algebraic bar vector. This proves convergence on the specified complex without interchanging an inverse limit with a bar realization. The projection remains the original augmentation. See Rational evaluation on the completed incoming bar, Proposition 1.

    The smooth realization is a different operation. For the specified smooth affine–right-YY object 𝒲\mathcal W, put

    ΦK(V)=𝒲K⊗YK𝕃V,K=ℂ((q)).\Phi_K(V)=\mathcal W_K\otimes^{\mathbb L}_{Y_K}V, \qquad K=\mathbb C((q)).

    To compute this derived tensor after forming ℬz(T)\mathcal B_z(T), use a separate algebraic outgoing bar over YKY_K. It receives no further Laurent completion. The completed spectral module is not assumed to be KK-flat over YKY_K.

    The evaluation map is fixed on these bars. If pp is an outgoing rational-current resolution word, it sends

    p⊗b0[b1|⋯|br]t⟼Δrat(p)b0[b1|⋯|br]t.p\otimes b_0[b_1|\cdots|b_r]t \longmapsto \Delta_{\rm rat}(p)b_0[b_1|\cdots|b_r]t.

    The map Δrat\Delta_{\rm rat} expands rational currents at the incoming points and splits their exterior principal parts. Its Laurent loss depends on pp, uniformly in the incoming length, letters and terminal vector. A vector in the outgoing algebraic bar uses finitely many such pp, so their bounds have a common minimum. Its restriction along the affine resolution is the original affine evaluation, usually denoted bM,Nb_{M,N}; the rational evaluation is denoted ηM,N\eta_{M,N}. Their construction precedes the theorem that they induce an equivalence.

    8.6 A comparison for any finite number of radial inputs

    Take d≥2d\geq2 ordered points and fix their shape by

    td−1=1,td=0,A0=ℂ[t1,…,td−2,(∏i<j(ti−tj))−1],t_{d-1}=1,\quad t_d=0,\qquad A_0=\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_{d-2}, (\prod_{i<j}(t_i-t_j))^{-1}],
    F=Frac⁡(A0),K=F((q)),ai=q−1ti.F=\operatorname{Frac}(A_0),\qquad K=F((q)),\qquad a_i=q^{-1}t_i.

    Thus qq measures inverse overall separation, while the tit_i describe the shape. Algebraic scalar extension to FF takes place before Laurent completion. For d=2d=2, F=ℂF=\mathbb C.

    For ordinary unbounded YFY_F-modules MiM_i, put T=Tot⊕︎⁡(M1⊗F⋯⊗FMd)T=\operatorname{Tot}_{\oplus}(M_1\otimes_F\cdots\otimes_FM_d). The corrected differential uses the pair sum

    R𝐚=∑i<jrij(ai−aj),S𝐚(T)=(T((q)),dT+ρT(R𝐚)).R_{\mathbf a}=\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}(a_i-a_j), \qquad S_{\mathbf a}(T)=(T((q)),d_T+\rho_T(R_{\mathbf a})).

    Every pair occurs, including nonconsecutive pairs. The outgoing action on either type of generator yn=Bna,ca,ny_n=B_n^a,c_{a,n} is

    Δ𝐚(yn)=∑i=1d∑m=0n(nm)qm−ntin−mym(i).\Delta_{\mathbf a}(y_n)= \sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{m=0}^n\binom nm q^{m-n}t_i^{n-m}y_m^{(i)}.

    To define the independent current complex, split rational currents into polynomial currents 𝔭=𝔤[u]\mathfrak p=\mathfrak g[u] and proper currents x/(u−ai)sx/(u-a_i)^s, s≥1s\geq1. “Proper” here means vanishing at infinity. Set

    C=⨁e≥0U(𝔫)e∗.C=\bigoplus_{e\geq0}U(\mathfrak n)_e^*.

    The energy pieces are finite-dimensional; this is their direct-sum dual. At proper exterior arity bb, use

    ℛd,b(V)=(CF⊗d⊗FΛb(𝔫F⊕︎d)∘⊗FV)((q)),\mathscr R_{d,b}(V)= \bigl(C_F^{\otimes d}\otimes_F \Lambda^b(\mathfrak n_F^{\oplus d})^{\circ}\otimes_F V\bigr)((q)),

    where ∘\circ likewise means the direct-sum dual of finite total-pole-index pieces. For a smooth affine test complex XX, define

    ℐdr(X;T)=∏a,b≥0∏e∈ℤHomK⁡(Λa𝔭K⊗KXe,ℛd,b(Tr+e−a−b)).\mathcal I_d^r(X;T)= \prod_{a,b\geq0}\prod_{e\in\mathbb Z} \operatorname{Hom}_K\!\left( \Lambda^a\mathfrak p_K\otimes_K X^e, \mathscr R_{d,b}(T^{r+e-a-b})\right).

    Its differential is the total Chevalley–Eilenberg and mapping-complex differential for the rational-current action. Each coefficient has finite cofree and proper-mode support. On a fixed exterior arity and finite polynomial/test stage it has a lower Laurent bound; the bound is a bound on the finite coordinate matrix and need not be uniform over other stages or arities. All displayed products are retained. This definition comes from current operations and their support conditions, independently of smooth realization.

    Let D𝒩(AK)D_{\mathcal N}(A_K) be the full subcategory of the original smooth derived category whose cohomology has jointly locally nilpotent positive currents: each cohomology vector is killed by all sufficiently long products of positive currents. Its maps are the ambient derived maps.

    Theorem — finite radial current comparison. Assume the specified coherent smooth affine–right-YY realization, its tensor–Hom adjunction and full unit for ordinary unbounded YY-modules, its algebraic cofree model and common mode-cutoff actions. Assume also that every bounded-below smooth complex with jointly locally nilpotent positive-current cohomology belongs to the localizing category generated by WKW_K, and that the derived ideal triangle expresses each YFY_F-module by two complexes inflated from UFU_F. Here inflation uses the augmentation YF→UFY_F\to U_F, and the localizing category is closed under shifts, cones and arbitrary coproducts. Then, for every finite d≥2d\geq2, every ordinary unbounded tuple M1,…,MdM_1,\ldots,M_d, and every X∈D𝒩(AK)X\in D_{\mathcal N}(A_K), the actual evaluation gives an equivalence

    ΞT(X):RHomSm⁡(AK)⁡(X,𝒲K⊗YK𝕃S𝐚(T))→∼ℐd(X;T).\Xi_T(X): R\operatorname{Hom}_{\operatorname{Sm}(A_K)} \bigl(X,\mathcal W_K\otimes^{\mathbb L}_{Y_K}S_{\mathbf a}(T)\bigr) \xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal I_d(X;T).

    The comparison retains the outgoing line action, all its specified higher compatibilities, and every additional commuting incoming right action. At the regular tuple it retains all dd incoming regular right actions. Its coefficient evaluations are the rational maps ηM1,…,Md\eta_{M_1,\ldots,M_d} and their original affine restrictions bM1,…,Mdb_{M_1,\ldots,M_d}. The theorem uses the bar and scalar-extension orders stated above. See The radial finite-puncture current recipient, equation (45).

    The proof begins with inputs inflated from UFU_F, so the ghosts act by zero. The proper-current complex then contracts at order zero by the energywise dual of the free Chevalley contraction. Cross-point terms have positive Laurent order and increase mode support by at most that order. Perturbation therefore preserves the required support. Composed with this contraction, the actual comparison is 1+A1+A, with AA of positive order, and has a coefficientwise geometric inverse.

    For bounded-below inputs, representability and the positive-current torsion theorem extend this calculation to every ambient test in D𝒩D_{\mathcal N}. Explicit truncation towers then handle unbounded inflated inputs; their componentwise stabilization does not require a bound uniform over the product factors of ℐd\mathcal I_d. Finally, the two inflated terms of the ideal triangle extend the equivalence to one arbitrary input at a time. There are finitely many such steps. No infinite incoming bar is moved through a continuous Hom, and no equality D𝒩=Loc⁡(WK)D_{\mathcal N}=\operatorname{Loc}(W_K) is required.

    8.7 Finite integral heads and separated values

    There is a second useful route to the regular comparison. Before inverting the separation discriminant, one can work over Rd=ℂ[a1,…,ad−1]R_d=\mathbb C[a_1,\ldots,a_{d-1}]. The protected coefficient complex is generated by seeds Δw𝒞w⊗d\Delta^w\mathscr C_w^{\otimes d}, where Δ=∏i<j(ai−aj)\Delta=\prod_{i<j}(a_i-a_j) and 𝒞w\mathscr C_w is the energy-ww relative dual of the line algebra. The discriminant powers compensate the pole budgets. Closing these seeds under the specified currents and derivatives gives actual integral coefficient and current-chain complexes.

    A finite head bounds top energy, proper pole budget and derivative order. Each such head is a bounded perfect relative complex, so its derived dual commutes with derived scalar base change. After separation, normalized head duals assemble into the explicit complex

    Dˆn=(⨁N(DN0)n)((q))⊕︎(⨁N(DN0)n−1)((q)),\widehat D^n= \left(\bigoplus_N(D_N^0)^n\right)((q)) \oplus\left(\bigoplus_N(D_N^0)^{n-1}\right)((q)),
    d(f,g)=(dDf,(RNfN+1−qfN)N−dDg).d(f,g)=\bigl(d_Df,(R_Nf_{N+1}-qf_N)_N-d_Dg\bigr).

    Here DN0D_N^0 is the normalized head dual and RNR_N its restriction matrix after removing the common q−1q^{-1} factor. This formula specifies finite head support at every coefficient and one common lower Laurent bound. It does not use the unrestricted algebraic dual of the infinite head union.

    Evaluation is the original tensor–Hom map

    η(p⊗f)(l)=(−1)|p||f|f(p⊗l).\eta(p\otimes f)(l)=(-1)^{|p||f|}f(p\otimes l).

    For fixed pp, insertion changes the head NN to N+c(p)N+c(p). Normalization gives a Laurent loss depending on pp, independent of NN. Evaluation and its homotopies therefore extend to the completed head complexes. For the full incoming bar, the stronger estimate is uniform in incoming length, including arbitrarily long words of energy zero. These estimates identify the separated head construction with the same evaluation used above. The two occupied-vacuum orders also have actual completed comparison roofs at the regular output test, retaining the surviving regular action. See Integral kernels and the separated comparison diagrams, §§1–3.

    This separation of domains has a geometric consequence. A collision fibre sets a factor of Δ\Delta to zero, whereas the separated Laurent chart has inverted Δ\Delta. Derived collision maps are obtained from the integral finite heads before that inversion. They cannot be obtained by substituting a collision into every vector of the separated Laurent complex.

    8.8 Common radial sewing and a failed substitution

    The finite-point theorem permits a definite form of sewing: the original kernels can be composed along any finite binary tree on the same radial domain. The translation τx\tau_x of the source algebra YY is defined on either generator yn=Bnay_n=B_n^a or yn=ca,ny_n=c_{a,n} by

    τx(yn)=∑m=0n(nm)xn−mym,\tau_x(y_n)=\sum_{m=0}^n\binom nm x^{n-m}y_m,

    and extended multiplicatively. For fixed modes its kernel identities are rational identities,

    (τx⊗1)r(y)=r(y+x),(1⊗τx)r(y)=r(y−x).(\tau_x\otimes1)r(y)=r(y+x),\qquad (1\otimes\tau_x)r(y)=r(y-x).

    Continue those coefficients rationally before expanding radially. Each pair of leaves first meets at one vertex, so the tree contributes each term of R𝐚R_{\mathbf a} exactly once. Associative principal-part splitting gives the same rational and affine evaluations on the common completed incoming bar.

    A separately completed nested tensor need not have that domain. In a three-point shape chart,

    f=∑n≥0qnλ−n2∈ℂ(λ)((q)).f=\sum_{n\geq0}q^n\lambda^{-n^2}\in\mathbb C(\lambda)((q)).

    The substitution λ=zq\lambda=zq would give

    Its outer qq-orders have no lower bound, so it is not in ℂ((z−1))((q))\mathbb C((z^{-1}))((q)). The terms tend to zero before substitution and fail to do so afterwards. This is an obstruction to extending that substitution continuously to the entire radial field. It leaves the common radial sewing theorem intact and identifies the extra support estimate needed for a larger nested domain.

    Part III Operations and their domainsChapter 9 of 18

    9

    Ordered boundary operations and mixed theories

    Moving one insertion past another can change an operation even when the fields vary smoothly. The ordering region has a boundary, and differentiating its indicator produces a current on that boundary. When the insertions also have a holomorphic separation, this real boundary can meet a complex pole. The resulting contact term belongs to the operation.

    The problem is therefore more precise than extending a formula to coincident points. We need a space of distributions on which the formula, its differential and its compositions are all defined. We also need to distinguish a collision in the complex coordinate from a collision in both the real and complex coordinates. These distinctions lead to the relative complexes and height homotopies in this chapter.

    9.1 A boundary current from a mixed field theory

    On M=ℂz×ℝ≥0,tM=\mathbb C_z\times\mathbb R_{\geq0,t}, let

    d′=∂‾+dt,∂=dz∧∂z.d'=\bar\partial+d_t,\qquad \partial=dz\wedge\partial_z.

    A holomorphic–topological theory is holomorphic in zz and topological in the real direction. In its cohomological description, the antiholomorphic and real derivatives enter d′d'; holomorphic derivatives remain genuine operations.

    An abelian example has fields (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), where α\alpha is a form generated by dz‾,dtd\bar z,dt, while β\beta has one additional factor dzdz. An ordinary form of degree pp in either summand has cohomological degree p−1p-1. The differential is

    Qκ(α,β)=(d′α,d′β+κ∂α).Q_\kappa(\alpha,\beta) =\bigl(d'\alpha,d'\beta+\kappa\partial\alpha\bigr).

    Since d′∂+∂d′=0d'\partial+\partial d'=0, its square is zero for every κ\kappa. The degree-zero fields are the partial connection aa and holomorphic one-form bb. Their quadratic action density is

    ℒκ=b∧d′a+κ2a∧∂a.\mathcal L_\kappa=b\wedge d'a+\frac{\kappa}{2}a\wedge\partial a.

    At κ=0\kappa=0, this is the holomorphic BF presentation: the field bb multiplies the partial curvature F=d′aF=d'a.

    The integrated action requires compact support. The Batalin–Vilkovisky pairing pairs the two field summands by wedge product and integration and is independent of κ\kappa. This pairing includes the odd ghost and antifield components of the complex; retaining only a,ba,b would omit the differential needed for the quantum identities.

    Impose the boundary condition ι∗α=0\iota^*\alpha=0, with β\beta free at the boundary. A compactly supported contraction in the normal direction identifies the boundary observables with their supported bulk realization. This is an instance of the free bulk–boundary construction of Gwilliam, Rabinovich and Williams, Factorization algebras and abelian CS/WZW-type correspondences (arXiv:2001.07888). With residue integration normalized by (2πi)−1∫(2\pi i)^{-1}\int, the resulting current has singular product

    J(z)J(w)∼−ℏκ(z−w)2.J(z)J(w)\sim-\frac{\hbar\kappa}{(z-w)^2}.

    At κ=0\kappa=0, that singular product vanishes, but the bulk pairing is still nondegenerate and all polynomial current fields and holomorphic jets remain. Thus the level of a boundary current is not the same datum as the nondegeneracy of the bulk field pairing. The construction and signs are developed in Holomorphic BF theory and its boundary current, particularly the theorems on the boundary map and current at every level.

    9.2 Fields as joint currents

    The boundary calculation fixes a local operator product. A distributional current model makes the support data for moving and composing such operations explicit. On the full space ℝ×ℂ\mathbb R\times\mathbb C, write XI=(ℝ×ℂ)IX_I=(\mathbb R\times\mathbb C)^I for the external insertion positions. The variables in the coefficient distributions remain independent, even when two external points coincide.

    This coefficient complex has two polarizations, called xx and pp. An internal mixed form of degree rr has cohomological degree r−2r-2 in the xx-polarization and r−1r-1 in the pp-polarization. On every compact set of external parameters, the xx-variables have a common compact support. A pp-variable can extend upward in height, but above a common collar height its current is independent of that height and has no dtdt-component. This is the meaning of upward-proper support here. Particle number is finite, and these finite operations are defined over ℂ[ℏ]\mathbb C[\hbar].

    On one coefficient variable, the internal differential is

    Q(fx)=(d′f)x,Q(gp)=−(d′g)p,δ(fx)=−(∂zf)p,δ(gp)=0.Q(f_x)=(d'f)_x,\qquad Q(g_p)=-(d'g)_p,\qquad \delta(f_x)=-(\partial_zf)_p,\qquad \delta(g_p)=0.

    With external forms placed first, the full differential is

    𝒟=dXI+Q+δ,(Q+δ)(ω⊗n)=(−1)|ω|ω⊗(Q+δ)n.\mathcal D=d_{X_I}+Q+\delta, \qquad (Q+\delta)(\omega\otimes n) =(-1)^{|\omega|}\omega\otimes(Q+\delta)n.

    The notation dXId_{X_I} denotes the mixed exterior derivative in the position variables. The coefficient differential and its shifts are part of this formula.

    The degree-zero ray and current families are denoted by Wˆi,Jˆi\widehat W_i,\widehat J_i; their degree-one descendant is pˆi\widehat p_i. They obey

    𝒟Wˆi=−pˆi,𝒟pˆi=𝒟Jˆi=0.\mathcal D\widehat W_i=-\widehat p_i,\qquad \mathcal D\widehat p_i=\mathcal D\widehat J_i=0.

    They are smooth families of distributions in the internal variables. Normal ordering means multiplication in independent internal variables followed by particle symmetrization. It introduces no extra contraction at coincident external endpoints.

    For nij=(tj−ti,zi−zj)n_{ij}=(t_j-t_i,z_i-z_j), the nonzero cross contractions are

    ⟨Wi,Jj⟩=−ℏb1(nij),⟨pi,Jj⟩=ℏQ1(nij),⟨Ji,Jj⟩=ℏE2(zi−zj).\langle W_i,J_j\rangle=-\hbar b_1(n_{ij}),\qquad \langle p_i,J_j\rangle=\hbar Q_1(n_{ij}),\qquad \langle J_i,J_j\rangle=\hbar E_2(z_i-z_j).

    Here Em(z)E_m(z) is the principal-value current z−mz^{-m}, QmQ_m is a scalar one-form kernel, and, off z=0z=0,

    b1(t,z)=12z(1+tt2+|z|2).b_1(t,z)=\frac{1}{2z} \left(1+\frac{t}{\sqrt{t^2+|z|^2}}\right).

    The height distinguishes the two sides of a complex collision. At positive height its singular part approaches 1/z1/z; at negative height it becomes regular near z=0z=0.

    A scalar distribution KK of finite order multiplies a smooth coefficient family FF by the joint-test formula

    ⟨KF,φ⟩=⟨K, q⟼⟨F(q),φ(q,⋅)⟩⟩.\langle KF,\varphi\rangle =\left\langle K,\ q\longmapsto \langle F(q),\varphi(q,\cdot)\rangle\right\rangle.

    Uniform support, collar and finite-order estimates make this a joint distribution. In particular, a relation between two expressions is an equality after all external and internal tests. A graph presentation is a way to compute the current, not additional data attached to it. This distinction is what permits the product in Composition on actual Gaussian images and their finite contact strata to accept its earlier output as a new input.

    9.3 Ordered poles and their complete differential

    Thus ∂‾Em=rm\bar\partial E_m=r_m. The first bulk kernel is the distributional one-form represented off the origin by

    For every m≥1m\geq1, define the higher kernels by holomorphic distributional differentiation:

    bm=(−1)m−1(m−1)!∂zm−1b1,Qm=(−1)m−1(m−1)!∂zm−1Q1.b_m=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\partial_z^{m-1}b_1, \qquad Q_m=\frac{(-1)^{m-1}}{(m-1)!}\partial_z^{m-1}Q_1.

    This is the same normalization as EmE_m. The scalar ray identities are

    Dbm=Qm+H(t)rm,DQm=−Cm,D=dt+∂‾.D b_m=Q_m+H(t)r_m,\qquad DQ_m=-C_m, \qquad D=d_t+\bar\partial.

    The term H(t)r1H(t)r_1 is the distributional contribution at the complex pole. Differentiating it gives C1C_1, which cancels DQ1DQ_1. This is the full identity D2b1=0D^2b_1=0. Omitting the real wall would destroy it.

    With many rays, the whole arrangement must be extended across its dependent collision loci. Multiplying independently extended factors on a common singular normal need not define a distribution. The scalar arrangement kernels use the following extension class.

    Work on a coordinate space V=Vt×VzV=V_t\times V_z, with VtV_t real and VzV_z complex. Let ℒ\mathscr L be the finite intersection-closed lattice of proper subspaces generated by the complex collision loci, mixed collision loci and gate walls. Its members are products of real-linear and complex-linear subspaces. At y∈Vy\in V, let L(y)L(y) be the intersection of the lattice members containing yy, or VV if there are none, and let πy:V→V/L(y)\pi_y:V\to V/L(y) be the quotient. If its real factor has dimension pyp_y and its complex factor has complex dimension kyk_y, the quotient has mixed dimension py+kyp_y+k_y.

    A normal current ω\omega is bihomogeneous of bidegree (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) if, including its form factors,

    gλ,θ∗ω=λαeiβθω,gλ,θ(t,z)=(λt,λeiθz),λ>0.g_{\lambda,\theta}^*\omega =\lambda^\alpha e^{i\beta\theta}\omega, \qquad g_{\lambda,\theta}(t,z)=(\lambda t,\lambda e^{i\theta}z), \quad\lambda>0.

    Its excess is α−β\alpha-\beta. A current is tame if near each yy it has a finite presentation

    ∑jηj∧πy∗ωj,\sum_j\eta_j\wedge\pi_y^*\omega_j,

    where ηj\eta_j are smooth mixed forms and ωj\omega_j are bihomogeneous normal currents of nonnegative excess. It is subcritical if, at every point of the lattice union, these models can be chosen with deg⁡ωj<py+ky\deg\omega_j<p_y+k_y. This bounds the normal model degree, which can be smaller than the total degree after multiplication by ηj\eta_j. The whole scalar arrangement has a unique extension in this class agreeing with its regular kernel; see Subcritical Q cycles and finite native Gaussian kernels, equation (1.4), Theorem 2.1 and Corollary 3.2. This fixes the scalar extension; a physical principle selecting that extension is a separate question.

    A supporting flat is described by a partition of the real coordinates and a partition of the complex coordinates. Compatibility means that the real partition refines the complex one: equality in height is imposed only within a complex block. Scalar rays and marked one-forms QmQ_m join distinct complex blocks. Gates H(h)H(h) compare real blocks inside a complex block. One also allows finite holomorphic derivatives of the top normal delta currents.

    For a set AA of marked edges, let pAp_A be the real rank of its height forms and kAk_A the complex rank of its complex forms. The nonzero admissible case requires |A|<pA+kA|A|<p_A+k_A for every nonempty marked subset; violating this inequality gives the zero whole kernel. A critical contact has

    |A|=pA+kA−1.|A|=p_A+k_A-1.

    The two ranks can differ. For example, Q1(s,u)∧Q1(t,u)Q_1(s,u)\wedge Q_1(t,u) has two independent real normals and one complex normal. With

    Ω2=πδ(s)δ(t)δℂ(u)ds∧dt∧du‾,\Omega_2=\pi\delta(s)\delta(t)\delta_{\mathbb C}(u) \,ds\wedge dt\wedge d\bar u,

    the complete gated current satisfies

    D[H(t−s)Q1(s,u)∧Q1(t,u)]=−12∂uΩ2.D\bigl[H(t-s)Q_1(s,u)\wedge Q_1(t,u)\bigr] =-\frac12\partial_u\Omega_2.

    The factor 1/21/2 is determined by the two complementary chambers. Their currents sum to the ungated current, whose derivative is −∂uΩ2-\partial_u\Omega_2; interchanging s,ts,t makes their two coefficients equal. This computation never assigns a value to H(0)H(0). A ray weight changes the residue: on the corresponding whole arrangement,

    D[Q1(s,u)∧Q1(t,u)b1(s,u)]=14∂u2Ω2.D\bigl[Q_1(s,u)\wedge Q_1(t,u)b_1(s,u)\bigr] =\frac14\partial_u^2\Omega_2.

    These formulas illustrate the weighted normal theorem, rather than multiplication of an existing point contact by a singular ray.

    Let ℳI\mathcal M_I be the actual finite span of these compatible scalar currents multiplied by finite normally ordered W,p,JW,p,J families and smooth external forms, including all allowed holomorphic normal jets. The following closure theorem is the basic algebraic input to moving the operations.

    Theorem — finite marked Ward calculus. With the stated compatible flats, internal gates, finite pole and jet orders, upward-proper coefficient support and canonical scalar extension, 𝒟ℳI⊆ℳI\mathcal D\mathcal M_I\subseteq\mathcal M_I. For a scalar coefficient KK with qq marked factors, its derivative consists of four finite sums:

    DK=ℬ(K)+𝒮(K)+𝒱(K)+𝒞(K).DK=\mathcal B(K)+\mathcal S(K)+\mathcal V(K)+\mathcal C(K).

    Here ℬ\mathcal B replaces a ray by an additional mark with sign (−1)q(-1)^q; 𝒮\mathcal S takes the residues of entire complex-parallel scalar classes; 𝒱\mathcal V takes the oriented real boundaries of whole simplified gates; and 𝒞\mathcal C is the sum over closed critical marked flats. Its coefficients are the annular moments of the whole weighted, gated normal kernel. The derivative of KFKF also includes (−1)qK𝒟F(-1)^qK\mathcal DF. Old normal degrees contribute their Koszul sign, and every residue differentiates the entire remaining coefficient and field family to the required finite normal order.

    The proof classifies all active normal strata. Removing an entire vanishing scalar class leaves proper tangent factors; the critical-normal calculation supplies the missing mixed contacts. Finite-order estimates justify each transpose against a joint test. Since the formula equals the actual distributional differential, it respects every relation between presentations of the same current. The precise statement is The finite marked Ward calculus on compatible collision flats, Theorems 4.1 and 7.1.

    The disjoint-label Gaussian product ⋆\star also closes on this space and is associative with its labelled signs. Its Ward defect

    𝔚(X,Y)=𝒟(X⋆Y)−(𝒟X)⋆Y−(−1)|X|X⋆(𝒟Y)\mathfrak W(X,Y)=\mathcal D(X\star Y) -(\mathcal DX)\star Y-(-1)^{|X|}X\star(\mathcal DY)

    is computable from the same formulas and is supported on cross complex collisions. Consequently 𝒟\mathcal D is not a derivation of this product. The defect is retained as operation data.

    9.4 Relative currents and a radial homotopy

    Let ZIZ_I be the union of physical pair diagonals, where both height and complex position coincide. Write ℳZ\mathcal M_Z for currents in ℳI\mathcal M_I supported there. The relative complex is

    ℱℳn=ℳIn⊕︎ℳZn+1,dF(α,γ)=(𝒟α+γ,−𝒟γ).\mathcal F_{\mathcal M}^n =\mathcal M_I^n\oplus\mathcal M_Z^{n+1}, \qquad d_F(\alpha,\gamma)=(\mathcal D\alpha+\gamma,-\mathcal D\gamma).

    Its second component records the supported correction to the first. For example, if GG is a gated complex normal current and FF its smooth tangent coefficient, the pair

    (GF,−DGF)(GF,-DG\,F)

    retains the real boundary of the gate. Its differential includes the derivative of FF; scalar closedness alone does not make the pair closed.

    The decomposition by supporting flats supplies a projection PZP_Z on this finite current space. It need not commute with 𝒟\mathcal D. The correct chain map is

    E(x)=((1−PZ)x,𝒟PZx−PZ𝒟x).E(x)=\bigl((1-P_Z)x,\mathcal DP_Zx-P_Z\mathcal Dx\bigr).

    With 𝖱(α,γ)=E(α)\mathsf R(\alpha,\gamma)=E(\alpha) and 𝖧(α,γ)=(0,PZα)\mathsf H(\alpha,\gamma)=(0,P_Z\alpha), direct calculation gives

    𝖱2=𝖱,1−𝖱=dF𝖧+𝖧dF.\mathsf R^2=\mathsf R,\qquad 1-\mathsf R=d_F\mathsf H+\mathsf H d_F.

    This retracts the displayed relative complex onto E(ℳI)E(\mathcal M_I). It leaves purely complex intersection currents in the first component. It does not contract the entire ambient space of coefficient distributions.

    A geometric homotopy requires an actual family. Consider the three-field circuit :W12:, :W2J2:, :J32::W_1^2:,\ :W_2J_2:,\ :J_3^2:, together with any finite disjoint set of mutually contracting, initially unmarked W,JW,J spectators. Set

    t0=t3,τ=t2−t1,σ=t3−t2,u=z1−z2,v=z2−z3.t_0=t_3,\quad \tau=t_2-t_1,\quad \sigma=t_3-t_2, \qquad u=z_1-z_2,\quad v=z_2-z_3.

    Scale the circuit heights by

    t1↦t0−λ(τ+σ),t2↦t0−λσ,t3↦t0,0<λ≤1,t_1\mapsto t_0-\lambda(\tau+\sigma),\qquad t_2\mapsto t_0-\lambda\sigma,\qquad t_3\mapsto t_0,\qquad 0<\lambda\leq1,

    leaving spectator heights and all complex coordinates unchanged. At positive scale this gives a distributional pullback. Its extension to zero is constructed as a limit of the full family, including parameter forms. In particular,

    d(t0−λσ)=dt0−λdσ−σdλ.d(t_0-\lambda\sigma) =dt_0-\lambda\,d\sigma-\sigma\,d\lambda.

    The walls remain present:

    δ(λℓ)d(λℓ)=λ−1δ(ℓ)(λdℓ+ℓdλ)=δ(ℓ)dℓ.\delta(\lambda\ell)\,d(\lambda\ell) =\lambda^{-1}\delta(\ell) (\lambda\,d\ell+\ell\,d\lambda) =\delta(\ell)\,d\ell.

    The last equality uses ℓδ(ℓ)=0\ell\delta(\ell)=0; it does not discard the parameter differential by convention.

    For this family the fixed relative support ZZ is the union of the three circuit mixed diagonals, times the full spectator parameter space. It does not include every spectator collision. The first component may acquire spectator contacts; only the second component is required to remain supported on ZZ.

    Theorem — radial circuit transport. On the actual span 𝒮\mathscr S of the complete first and successive circuit contacts, their stated spectator compositions, smooth form multiples and finite holomorphic derivatives, the positive-scale pullback has a unique continuous joint-current extension to zero. It extends as a chain family to 𝒱=𝒮+dF𝒮\mathscr V=\mathscr S+d_F\mathscr S. Its proper parameter integral gives

    HF(α,γ)=(hα,−hγ),h=∫01ι∂λ𝒫dλ,H_F(\alpha,\gamma)=(h\alpha,-h\gamma),\qquad h=\int_0^1\iota_{\partial_\lambda}\mathcal P\,d\lambda,
    dFHF+HFdF=id⁡−sp0⁡.d_FH_F+H_Fd_F=\operatorname{id}-\operatorname{sp}_0.

    Both endpoints and the homotopy take values in the original ambient relative current complex with the same ZZ. The three successive contact branches retain their full sum-zero relation, including unmatched fields, vacuum terms and all finite normal jets.

    The source restriction makes the limit possible. Unmarked tangent coefficients are strongly C1C^1 on the required joint-current stages. Positive-scale equality of two presentations then extends uniquely to zero, so the construction descends to actual currents. The chain identity on 𝒮+dF𝒮\mathscr S+d_F\mathscr S uses the combined full derivative, including the pp-descendants. It requires no separate endpoint value for every term in that derivative.

    There is a sharp limit to a stronger trace claim. For the whole kernel Kt=[b1(t,v)2]K_t=[b_1(t,v)^2], its symmetric second difference, tested against v2χ(|v|2)v^2\chi(|v|^2), contains

    12(t2+ρ2).\frac{1}{2(t^2+\rho^2)}.

    Its radial integral is πlog⁡(1/|t|)+O(1)\pi\log(1/|t|)+O(1). Thus a general C2C^2 trace without a retained real normal is false. When every ray retains an independent spectator-height form, a stronger C2C^2 theorem and continuous single-mark traces hold. The radial circuit theorem uses the weaker bounds it needs. Its endpoint still remembers the original gates, walls and labels; it is not an operation depending only on the fused point. See A common radial height family for the first circuit and its spectator compositions, Theorem 1.1.

    9.5 Changing endpoint profiles

    A normal contraction also depends on a compact profile. Let pp integrate along an interval and let sa,sbs_a,s_b be sections defined by normalized profiles θa,θb\theta_a,\theta_b. Then

    Tba=1+(sb−sa)p,TcbTba=Tca,Tab=Tba−1.T_{ba}=1+(s_b-s_a)p,\qquad T_{cb}T_{ba}=T_{ca},\qquad T_{ab}=T_{ba}^{-1}.

    This transports the entire source and root map, not only their cohomology classes. A quantum operation must also transport its local pairing.

    For a planar disk DD and interval II, take the endpoint coefficient complex ℰc=Ωc∙(D×I)[2]\mathcal E_c=\Omega_c^\bullet(D\times I)[2] with b(u,v)=ν∫u∧vb(u,v)=\nu\int u\wedge v, with ν≠0\nu\ne0. Put A=(sb−sa)pA=(s_b-s_a)p and T=1+AT=1+A. Since both AuAu and AvAv contain dtdt,

    b(Tu,Tv)−b(u,v)=b(Au,v)+b(u,Av).b(Tu,Tv)-b(u,v)=b(Au,v)+b(u,Av).

    This defect can be nonzero. Choose a compact planar function ϕ\phi, a compact planar two-form ψ\psi, and real distinct profiles, with ∫Dϕψ≠0\int_D\phi\psi\ne0. For u=ϕ(θb−θa)u=\phi(\theta_b-\theta_a) and v=ψθadtv=\psi\theta_a\,dt, it equals

    ν(∫Dϕψ)(∫I(θb−θa)2dt)≠0.\nu\left(\int_D\phi\psi\right) \left(\int_I(\theta_b-\theta_a)^2dt\right)\ne0.

    The bare symmetric extension of TT therefore does not generally preserve the unchanged quantum differential.

    There is an explicit corrected transport. Let Πa,Πb\Pi_a,\Pi_b be the signed local primitives. The operator ∂Π\partial_\Pi contracts pairs of symmetric field factors with Π\Pi, and Ea=exp⁡(∂Πa)E_a=\exp(\partial_{\Pi_a}) changes from quantum to creation coordinates. Retain the cumulative cross pairings ca,cbc_a,c_b. Under the actual identity T∗cb=caT^*c_b=c_a, the map is

    GT=Eb−1Sym⁡(T)Ea=Sym⁡(T)exp⁡(−∂T∗Πb−Πa).G_T=E_b^{-1}\operatorname{Sym}(T)E_a =\operatorname{Sym}(T) \exp\!\bigl(-\partial_{\,T^*\Pi_b-\Pi_a}\bigr).

    It acts on the full fixed-field completed kernels, transports each source η\eta to TηT\eta, and preserves the full source–target matrix differential. The contraction exponential is finite at fixed field number. A word operation ff in these coordinates has linear part TY−1fTXT_Y^{-1}fT_X and the corresponding pairing correction. It agrees with the unchanged operation only when the actual unmatched-map square and primitive identities hold. Independent changes in two disjoint input bands generally cannot be absorbed by one output profile shear. These statements are proved in Local pairing defects and profile-labelled Gaussian operations.

    Higher refinement homotopies have their own continuity conditions. The normalized finite cubes and their evaluation mates act on mixed words with one Laurent lower bound before all state-energy and bar-length products. Profile paths and exponent distributions are algebraic at fixed indices. Finite coalgebra supports are chosen from right to left, before the still-free state products to their left; terminal coefficient and form slots remain independent until balancing. Constant finite-dimensional commuting charge profiles, including Jordan profiles, retain their full matrix Hom complexes on this domain.

    This positive theorem is compatible with a concrete obstruction on the larger energy-product domain. In the neutral creation algebra, let Ji,nJ_{i,n} have energy n+1n+1, let ci,nc_{i,n} be a ghost of energy nn, and let ss denote bar suspension. The specified normalized binary refinement cell satisfies

    K(sc1,0|s(3(z1−z3)n+1(z2−z3)n+1c2,0J3,n2))=s1.\overline K\!\left( sc_{1,0}\mid s\!\left(3(z_1-z_3)^{n+1}(z_2-z_3)^{n+1} c_{2,0}J_{3,n}^{\,2}\right)\right)=s1.

    Here s1s1 is the length-one bar state of the algebra unit; it is distinct from the empty word. The inputs tend to zero in the product over energy blocks, while the output is the same nonzero unit. Hence this cell has no continuous extension preserving those values to a Hausdorff target that retains the unit. In the logarithmic frame zi=b+t−1tiz_i=b+t^{-1}t_i, the multiplier has order −2(n+1)-2(n+1). The sequence therefore has no common Laurent lower bound. The obstruction concerns the larger source topology, and does not invalidate the normalized cubes and cap mates on their stated mixed Laurent domain.

    9.6 Two complex dimensions

    The geometry changes when the holomorphic space is ℂ2\mathbb C^2. Its volume form dz1∧dz2dz_1\wedge dz_2 couples two holomorphic directions, and current anomalies involve a cubic invariant rather than the quadratic level of a curve current. Higher current algebras and their free-field realizations are developed by Gwilliam and Williams in Higher Kac–Moody algebras and symmetries of holomorphic field theories (arXiv:1810.06534).

    A concrete family uses internal formal variables x,yx,y, distinct from the spatial z1,z2z_1,z_2. Put 𝔪=(x,y)⊂ℂ[[x,y]]\mathfrak m=(x,y)\subset\mathbb C[[x,y]] and

    VN=𝔪/𝔪N+1,𝔤N=𝔪2/𝔪N+2,ρN(f)g=fxgy−fygx.V_N=\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^{N+1},\qquad \mathfrak g_N=\mathfrak m^2/\mathfrak m^{N+2},\qquad \rho_N(f)g=f_xg_y-f_yg_x.

    The estimate {𝔪a,𝔪b}⊆𝔪a+b−2\{\mathfrak m^a,\mathfrak m^b\}\subseteq\mathfrak m^{a+b-2} makes the action well defined. Quadratic Hamiltonians preserve internal degree; higher ones raise it. On the first jet, the quadratic 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2 action has h=diag⁡(1,−1)h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1), so Tr⁡(h2)=2\operatorname{Tr}(h^2)=2 while Tr⁡(h3)=0\operatorname{Tr}(h^3)=0. The full symmetric cubic trace vanishes on every VNV_N. Degree-raising blocks cannot contribute to a closed trace, and the invariant pairings on the remaining quadratic blocks give the required reversal identity.

    For every finite NN and positive heat scale, this cancellation produces a nontrivial quantum higher Lie current map from Ωc0,∙(ℂ2,𝔤N)\Omega_c^{0,\bullet}(\mathbb C^2,\mathfrak g_N) to the compact quadratic distribution observables of the free matter theory. Its components satisfy the master equation, with formal ℏ\hbar and completion in background weight. This is the finite-current theorem of Hamiltonian jets and quantum currents. The cancellation concerns complete scalar wheels; individual ordered traces need not vanish.

    The ambient observables cannot simply be projected by deleting higher matter modes. For a removed dual pair b,gb,g with Batalin–Vilkovisky bracket {b,g}=1\{b,g\}=1, deletion gives r(b)=r(g)=0r(b)=r(g)=0 but r(1)=1r(1)=1. It is not a bracket-preserving map. The current-generated inverse systems use their own degree-triangular structure.

    There is a further geometric distinction. The internal matrix action fixes the spatial point. For actual holomorphic F,gF,g, let HF=(∂z1F)∂z2−(∂z2F)∂z1H_F=(\partial_{z_1}F)\partial_{z_2}-(\partial_{z_2}F)\partial_{z_1}. Taylor expansion in internal jet variables ξ1,ξ2\xi_1,\xi_2 gives

    jN+(HFg)=HF(z)⋅∂zjN+g+ρN(Fz≥2)jN+g.j_N^+(H_Fg) =H_F(z)\cdot\partial_zj_N^+g +\rho_N(F_z^{\geq2})j_N^+g.

    Here jN+j_N^+ is the positive Taylor jet through order NN, and Fz≥2F_z^{\geq2} is the Taylor part of FF of degrees two through N+1N+1. If F=z1F=z_1, g=z22g=z_2^2, and N=1N=1, the matrix term vanishes but the transport term sends 2z2ξ22z_2\xi_2 to 2ξ22\xi_2. A comparison with geometric Hamiltonian currents must retain that transport term and the relations defining holonomic jets.

    9.7 Compact comparison and prescribed lower homotopies

    Local current identities can isolate a global comparison without settling it. In the six-field elliptic cubic construction, let Aϵ:N→𝒴A_\epsilon:N\to\mathcal Y be the original compact output and Eϵ:Jq→𝒴E_\epsilon:J_q\to\mathcal Y the separately specified evaluation. The subscript qq labels a selected collision normal. The signed contraction N⇄JqN\rightleftarrows J_q has section jqj_q, projection gqg_q, and homotopy HqH_q. A further root–central contraction Jq⇄𝒢J_q\rightleftarrows\mathscr G has section jrj_r, projection grg_r, and homotopy hrh_r. The target retains the central outputs, both harmonic components and the full parameter-form coefficients. Let δu\delta_u be the degree-one unreduced contact from the prescribed six-field source, and δc=gqδu\delta_c=g_q\delta_u its projected contact. On their common actual domain, the comparison is

    Aϵδu−Eϵδc=∂ℒϵ+γϵgrδc,γϵ=Aϵjqjr−Eϵjr,A_\epsilon\delta_u-E_\epsilon\delta_c =\partial\mathcal L_\epsilon+\gamma_\epsilon g_r\delta_c, \qquad \gamma_\epsilon=A_\epsilon j_qj_r-E_\epsilon j_r,
    ℒϵ=AϵHqδu+(Aϵjq−Eϵ)hrδc.\mathcal L_\epsilon =A_\epsilon H_q\delta_u+(A_\epsilon j_q-E_\epsilon)h_r\delta_c.

    The boundary ∂\partial is the full Hom differential, so it includes the source differential on nonclosed inputs. The unresolved compact map is γϵ\gamma_\epsilon on the original supported contact image. A trace that kills its value would prove only a traced statement.

    Finite polynomial Green-boundary limits and their four-supported compositions are available with fixed finite polynomial and jet degrees, the original order of width limits and all source-contact terms. Selected scalar unit and section rows also have vanishing objectwise first-comparison values. That scalar sector is not a subcomplex: its coefficient differential produces antiholomorphic descendants. Those descendants remain in the Hom identities.

    The cylinder map from the canonical normal complex to the original normal complex is a separate required arrow, especially on unsupported homotopy outputs. A coordinate isomorphism of finite normal currents does not define it. A cubic compatibility for an operation Ω=∑iℏiΩi\Omega=\sum_i\hbar^i\Omega_i and map P=∑jℏjPjP=\sum_j\hbar^jP_j retains the entire coefficient

    Ω0P3+Ω1P2+Ω2P1+Ω3P0.\Omega_0P_3+\Omega_1P_2+\Omega_2P_1+\Omega_3P_0.

    Likewise, a cubic homotopy must preserve the prescribed lower homotopies. If the Hom differential is ∂0+ℏ∂1+⋯\partial_0+\hbar\partial_1+\cdots, correcting lower coefficients S0,S1,S2S_0,S_1,S_2 contributes

    −∂1S2−∂2S1−∂3S0-\partial_1S_2-\partial_2S_1-\partial_3S_0

    at order ℏ3\hbar^3. These terms explain why a local normalization or one scalar contact cannot settle the relative cubic attachment. The remaining question is an equality of specified maps with their supported domains and lower homotopies. Analytic sewing asks for exactly this kind of control when the local constructions are glued.

    Part III Operations and their domainsChapter 10 of 18

    10

    Analytic sewing and conformal blocks

    Three local fields can be combined by first combining the first two, or by first combining the last two. In an algebra, associativity compares two compositions that are already defined. For conformal fields, even forming those compositions requires an infinite sum over descendant states and often an integral over intermediate representations. The first question is therefore where the sums converge. The second is whether their values can be used as inputs to another operation.

    These questions lead to different constructions. Finite words of Virasoro fields admit analytic sewings on explicit completed spaces, with unit maps and coherent changes of parentheses. There is also a complete, dense input space assigned functorially to a large class of their output representations. Yet an actual collision of two primary fields can leave that input space. Understanding this distinction is necessary before interpreting analytic fusion as a tensor product of arbitrary representations, and before using it to prepare the states required by a field theory.

    10.1 Virasoro representations and domains of fields

    Fix a real central charge c>1c>1. The Virasoro relations are

    [Lm,Ln]=(m−n)Lm+n+c12(m3−m)δm+n,0id.[L_m,L_n]=(m-n)L_{m+n} +\frac{c}{12}(m^3-m)\delta_{m+n,0}\,\mathrm{id}.

    For a positive principal label pp, let HpH_p be the Hilbert completion of the irreducible highest-weight module with highest vector Ωp\Omega_p and weight

    hp=c−124+p2,L0Ωp=hpΩp,LnΩp=0(n>0).h_p=\frac{c-1}{24}+p^2, \qquad L_0\Omega_p=h_p\Omega_p, \qquad L_n\Omega_p=0\quad(n>0).

    Its level-NN subspace has energy hp+Nh_p+N. A descendant is a vector obtained by applying negative modes to Ωp\Omega_p. Positive Hilbert forms control convergence; the contractions used in sewing are the complex-bilinear invariant forms, with their inverse Gram matrices. These two uses of a pairing must be distinguished.

    Write Ep=L0(p)E_p=L_0^{(p)}. For real tt, the energy space Hp[t]H_p[t] has norm

    ‖v‖Hp[t]2=∑N≥0e2t(hp+N)‖vN‖Hp2.\|v\|_{H_p[t]}^2 =\sum_{N\ge0}e^{2t(h_p+N)}\|v_N\|_{H_p}^2.

    For t>0t>0, this is the domain of etEpe^{tE_p}; negative tt gives a weaker completion. The entire-energy input space is

    ℰp=⋂n≥1Hp[n],\mathscr E_p=\bigcap_{n\ge1}H_p[n],

    with the topology defined by these norms. Every finite descendant belongs to it. The intersection permits arbitrary positive exponential energy weights, which is stronger than requiring smoothness under finitely many powers of L0L_0.

    For finitely many labels, the completed projective tensor product

    E𝐩=ℰp1⊗ˆπ⋯⊗ˆπℰpdE_{\mathbf p} =\mathscr E_{p_1}\widehat\otimes_\pi\cdots \widehat\otimes_\pi\mathscr E_{p_d}

    is exactly the space of coefficient arrays uN1,…,Ndu_{N_1,\ldots,N_d} for which

    ∑𝐍e2a∑i(hpi+Ni)‖u𝐍‖2<∞for every a≥1.\sum_{\mathbf N}e^{2a\sum_i(h_{p_i}+N_i)} \|u_{\mathbf N}\|^2<\infty \quad\text{for every }a\ge1.

    Thus the input includes entangled arrays, not just finite sums of separated vectors. The equality of topologies follows from the subexponential growth of descendant multiplicities: an arbitrarily small additional exponential weight makes the inclusions between Hilbert stages trace-class. Cauchy–Schwarz then bounds the projective tensor seminorm by a stronger Hilbert-array norm. This is the completion on which the subsequent operations act. Radial comb sewings of arbitrary finite length, §“The entire finite-word source”.

    A conformal block on a punctured curve is a multilinear functional satisfying the Ward identities: the sum of the local Virasoro actions of a meromorphic vector field vanishes, with the contragredient action at an outgoing puncture. For example, expanding a rational vector field near a puncture at aia_i gives

    f(ai+w)=∑n=−Mi∞fi,nwn+1,Li(f)=∑n=−Mi∞fi,nLn(i).f(a_i+w)=\sum_{n=-M_i}^{\infty}f_{i,n}w^{n+1}, \qquad L_i(f)=\sum_{n=-M_i}^{\infty}f_{i,n}L_n^{(i)}.

    The finite principal part uses finitely many modes. The regular part is an infinite positive-mode series; its exponential coefficient growth is absorbed by a stronger entire-energy input norm. A formal Ward identity becomes an analytic identity only after this series and the sewing contractions have been defined continuously.

    The normalized binary operation, with the stationary input first, is

    μa,b(z)(u,v)(p)=21/4C0(a,b,p)Ipb,a(v,z)u.\mu_{a,b}(z)(u,v)(p) =2^{1/4}\sqrt{C_0(a,b,p)}\,I_p^{b,a}(v,z)u.

    Here Ipb,aI_p^{b,a} is the normalized Virasoro intertwining field and z≠0z\ne0 has a chosen logarithm. The three-point normalization and spectral measure are fixed input data of the normalized boundary hypothesis. To specify them, put

    Q=(c−1)/6,𝔟+𝔟−1=Q.Q=\sqrt{(c-1)/6},\qquad \mathfrak b+\mathfrak b^{-1}=Q.

    Choose 0<𝔟≤10<\mathfrak b\le1 for c≥25c\ge25, and 𝔟=eiθ\mathfrak b=e^{i\theta}, 0<θ<π/20<\theta<\pi/2, for 1<c<251<c<25. Let Γ𝔟\Gamma_{\mathfrak b} be Barnes' double Gamma function with periods 𝔟,𝔟−1\mathfrak b,\mathfrak b^{-1}, normalized by Γ𝔟(Q/2)=1\Gamma_{\mathfrak b}(Q/2)=1, with its continuation in Re⁡𝔟>0\operatorname{Re}\mathfrak b>0. Then

    C0(p1,p2,p3)=Γ𝔟(2Q)2Γ𝔟(Q)3∏ϵ1,ϵ2,ϵ3=±1Γ𝔟(Q/2+i∑j=13ϵjpj)∏j=13Γ𝔟(Q+2ipj)Γ𝔟(Q−2ipj),C_0(p_1,p_2,p_3)= \frac{\Gamma_{\mathfrak b}(2Q)} {\sqrt2\,\Gamma_{\mathfrak b}(Q)^3} \frac{\displaystyle\prod_{\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon_3=\pm1} \Gamma_{\mathfrak b}\!\left(Q/2+i\sum_{j=1}^3\epsilon_jp_j\right)} {\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^3 \Gamma_{\mathfrak b}(Q+2ip_j)\Gamma_{\mathfrak b}(Q-2ip_j)},
    dν(p)=m𝔟(p)dp,m𝔟(p)=4sinh⁡(2π𝔟p)sinh⁡(2πp/𝔟).d\nu(p)=m_{\mathfrak b}(p)\,dp,\qquad m_{\mathfrak b}(p)= 4\sinh(2\pi\mathfrak b p)\sinh(2\pi p/\mathfrak b).

    For real principal labels these quantities are positive, and the binary map uses the positive square root of C0C_0. The measure is ρ0(p)dp/2\rho_0(p)\,dp/\sqrt2, where ρ0=2m𝔟\rho_0=\sqrt2\,m_{\mathfrak b} is the vacuum-resolution density; the factor 2\sqrt2 is therefore not absorbed into dνd\nu. These conventions are invariant under 𝔟↔𝔟−1\mathfrak b\leftrightarrow\mathfrak b^{-1}. Virasoro fusion construction, §11.0 and equation (13.2).

    The primary component is

    gz(p)=21/4C0(a,b,p)zhp−ha−hb.g_z(p)=2^{1/4}\sqrt{C_0(a,b,p)} z^{h_p-h_a-h_b}.

    The exponent is forced by L0L_0-covariance. The normalization and spectral measure carry further information: changing them changes the Hilbert comparison between channels.

    Throughout the sewing results below, the normalized boundary hypothesis is retained: for algebraic external states, the two four-point inverse-Gram sewings converge in their respective channel discs, their marked channel vectors lie in the canonical spectral L2L^2 spaces, and the two are related by the specified real unitary fusion transformation. We also retain the normalized positive-label pentagon when comparing trees. These are substantive hypotheses. The role of quantum-group harmonic analysis in constructing fusion transformations is developed by Ponsot and Teschner, Liouville bootstrap via harmonic analysis on a noncompact quantum group (arXiv:hep-th/9911110); analytic continuation of fusion coefficients alone does not supply every completed-source estimate used here.

    10.2 Finite uncut sewings

    The analytic estimate that permits iteration has two independent energy margins. If

    r>−log⁡|z|>s,r>-\log|z|>s,

    there is a finite tt such that the actual kernel

    Kz(a,b;p)=esEpμa,b(z)(e−rEa⊗e−tEb)K_z(a,b;p) =e^{sE_p}\mu_{a,b}(z) (e^{-rE_a}\otimes e^{-tE_b})

    is Hilbert–Schmidt and satisfies

    ‖Kz(a,b;p)‖HS2≤Ce−γ(a2+b2+p2),γ>0.\|K_z(a,b;p)\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2 \le C e^{-\gamma(a^2+b^2+p^2)},\qquad \gamma>0.

    The constants are uniform on compact logarithmic coordinate sets with strict margins, uniformly in the positive labels and locally uniformly in c>1c>1. This estimate concerns the canonical kernel at every label. It never evaluates an arbitrary spectral L2L^2 class at a point. All subsequent assertions retain this two-radius estimate and its normal descendant-tail bounds. Radial comb sewings, Lemmas FC.1–FC.2.

    Place dd inputs at 0,a2,…,ad0,a_2,\ldots,a_d, with

    0<|a2|<⋯<|ad|.0<|a_2|<\cdots<|a_d|.

    The left-associated operation first combines the first two inputs, then combines that result with the third, and continues. Keep the intermediate labels k2,…,kd−1k_2,\ldots,k_{d-1} as resolved multiplicities. Its output space is

    𝒵d[s]=L2(dν(k2)⋯dν(kd−1)dν(e);He[s]).\mathcal Z_d[s] =L^2\!\left(d\nu(k_2)\cdots d\nu(k_{d-1})d\nu(e); H_e[s]\right).

    No energy weight is imposed on a retained multiplicity label.

    Theorem 10.1 (finite analytic sewing). Under the normalized boundary hypothesis and the two-radius estimates above, fix d≥2d\ge2, s∈ℝs\in\mathbb R, positive external labels, and

    K⋐{0<|a2|<⋯<|ad|,s<−log⁡|ad|}K\Subset\{0<|a_2|<\cdots<|a_d|,\; s<-\log|a_d|\}

    on a logarithmic coordinate cover. There is a finite input exponent tKt_K for which the actual left-associated sewing is a holomorphic Hilbert–Schmidt family

    Cd(𝐚):⨂ˆi=1d2Hpi[tK]⟶𝒵d[s].C_d(\mathbf a): \widehat\bigotimes_{i=1}^{d}{}_{\!2}H_{p_i}[t_K] \longrightarrow\mathcal Z_d[s].

    It therefore acts continuously on E𝐩E_{\mathbf p}. Every internal and output spectrum and every descendant level is uncut. Finite cutoffs converge normally in this operator norm on smaller compact sets. The scalar factor is exactly

    2(d−1)/4∏vC0(kv,L,kv,R,kv),2^{(d-1)/4}\sqrt{\prod_{v}C_0(k_{v,L},k_{v,R},k_v)},

    with one factor for each binary vertex. Bounds are uniform in the external positive labels and locally uniform in cc. They need not be uniform in dd, near collisions, or at the boundary of the strict output inequality. Radial comb sewings, Theorem FC.3.

    The mechanism is visible at the third insertion. The inequalities |a2|<|a3||a_2|<|a_3| permit an intermediate exponent

    −log⁡|a3|<r<−log⁡|a2|.-\log|a_3|<r<-\log|a_2|.

    The first collision produces an output in the stage rr; the second vertex receives that same stage. Its Gaussian spectral bound is integrable against the canonical measure. Strengthening the input stages slightly leaves geometric decay in the descendant tails. Repeating this argument finitely many times constructs the entire word. The intermediate output is used through its proved stage, rather than through an operation postulated on its whole distributional completion.

    Every planar binary tree has an independently convergent hierarchical corner, obtained by taking each subcluster sufficiently small compared with its parent separation. Four-point fusion maps compare these corners. Disjoint rotations commute, and the normalized pentagon identifies the two reassociation paths among the five trees on four ordered leaves. If FT′,TF_{T',T} denotes the comparison from the retained-label space of TT to that of T′T', the two path products have the same source and target and agree. These are actual unitaries on the intermediate labels, acting trivially on the final representation. Their coherent analytic continuations agree with the left-associated sewing on the stated common domains. A non-left-associated raw series still has its own convergence domain. Independent finite-tree sewings and their coherence, FT.1–FT.4.

    10.3 The vacuum as an input and as an output

    The vacuum representation has highest weight zero and is a separate object from the positive principal family. Its highest vector Ω\Omega obeys L−1Ω=0L_{-1}\Omega=0. Write vN∈VNv_N\in V_N for its orthogonal level components. The fixed weighted vacuum Hilbert space is

    Vσ={v=∑N≥0vN:‖v‖Vσ2=∑N≥0σN2‖vN‖V2<∞}.V_\sigma=\left\{v=\sum_{N\ge0}v_N: \|v\|_{V_\sigma}^2 =\sum_{N\ge0}\sigma_N^2\|v_N\|_V^2<\infty\right\}.

    To control all field insertions, take its graph space

    G={v:‖Dv‖Vσ<∞ for every finite Virasoro word D}.G=\{v:\|Dv\|_{V_\sigma}<\infty \text{ for every finite Virasoro word }D\}.

    Its seminorms are qD(v)=‖Dv‖Vσq_D(v)=\|Dv\|_{V_\sigma}, so the weight is applied at the output level after DD. The weights are the prescribed ones from the vacuum estimates: σ0=1\sigma_0=1 and σN=23NeN2MN\sigma_N=2^{3N}e^{N^2}M_N, with the fixed nondecreasing maximum MN≥1M_N\ge1 of the annular-action weights and finite three-vacuum Ward tensor norms specified in A common rapid completion for all vacuum sectors, equation (A.3). Replacing this graph topology by an arbitrary weak vacuum completion changes the theorem.

    One vacuum input may be inserted anywhere in a fixed finite positive word, on the full source

    G⊗ˆπℰp1⊗ˆπ⋯⊗ˆπℰpr.G\widehat\otimes_\pi\mathscr E_{p_1} \widehat\otimes_\pi\cdots\widehat\otimes_\pi\mathscr E_{p_r}.

    The unit coefficients are one. With the stationary input written first, the binary unit formulas are

    Γp,V(z)(v,Ω)=v,ΓV,p(z)(Ω,v)=ezL−1v.\Gamma_{p,V}(z)(v,\Omega)=v, \qquad \Gamma_{V,p}(z)(\Omega,v)=e^{zL_{-1}}v.

    The second formula includes the translation of the remaining insertion. Its inverse is applied only on a stage on which that translation is defined. When the vacuum is first, the reflected construction gives the separate output range 𝒵[−b]\mathcal Z[-b], b>log⁡2b>\log2, on the normalized real interior and local complex neighbourhoods. Mixed trees have their own convergent corners and inherit comparisons from the positive tree obtained by removing the vacuum leaf. One vacuum input in an arbitrary finite word, equation FV.12 and Theorem FV.3.

    Vacuum output requires another map. The strong dual Gb′G'_b, equipped with uniform convergence on bounded subsets of GG, receives a nonzero three-positive-input conformal block. At positions 0,z,10,z,1, its primary coefficient is

    21/4C0(A,B,C)zhC−hA−hB(1−z)hA−hB−hC.2^{1/4}\sqrt{C_0(A,B,C)} z^{h_C-h_A-h_B}(1-z)^{h_A-h_B-h_C}.

    The construction extends throughout |z|<1,|1−z|<1|z|<1, |1-z|<1, including 0<z<10<z<1. For every fixed finite positive word of length d≥3d\ge3, a specified rooted vacuum channel similarly exists on the real ordered interior and complex neighbourhoods. It retains d−3d-3 uncut internal spectra as a Hilbert multiplicity MM, with target

    V(M)=(M∨⊗ˆπG)b′.V(M)=(M^\vee\widehat\otimes_\pi G)'_b.

    The proof first constructs fixed-label canonical kernels, then uses annular composition and Möbius transport. For d>3d>3, equality with every differently rooted vacuum channel is a further question. A vacuum output for finite positive words.

    These outputs force the vacuum into any proposed common target. On the specified closed finite products of positive outputs, L0L_0 is onto and invertible. A continuous Virasoro map from such a space to Gb′G'_b must have zero highest-vacuum coefficient, since that coefficient annihilates the image of L0L_0. Vacuum cyclicity then kills every descendant coefficient. Thus the map is zero, whereas the displayed vacuum-output block is nonzero. The positive output alone cannot represent it.

    10.4 A common intrinsic input space

    It is natural to ask whether the input topology can be recovered from the output representation itself. The relevant outputs have several different topologies. For continuous positive spectral sections, use the common oscillator realization ℱ=⨁ˆN≥0ℱN\mathcal F=\widehat\bigoplus_{N\ge0}\mathcal F_N, with energy E(p)=hp+NE(p)=h_p+N, and put

    𝒞a={f:eaE(p)f(p)∈C0([0,∞);ℱ)},𝒫G=lim→m≥1⁡𝒞−m.\mathscr C_a =\{f:e^{aE(p)}f(p)\in C_0([0,\infty);\mathcal F)\}, \qquad \mathscr P_G=\varinjlim_{m\ge1}\mathscr C_{-m}.

    Here C0C_0 denotes continuous functions vanishing at infinity, and each stage has its weighted supremum norm. It is unrelated to the three-point constant C0(a,b,p)C_0(a,b,p). The input of 𝒫G\mathscr P_G is ⋂n≥1𝒞n\bigcap_{n\ge1}\mathscr C_n.

    For a specified positive spectral object YY, with its scalar measure νY\nu_Y and measurable Hilbert multiplicities MpM_p, let

    ℋa(Y)=L2(dνY(p);Mp⊗ˆ2Hp[a]),𝒢(Y)=(⋂n≥1ℋn(Y∨))b′.\mathcal H_a(Y) =L^2(d\nu_Y(p);M_p\widehat\otimes_2H_p[a]), \qquad \mathscr G(Y)= \left(\bigcap_{n\ge1}\mathcal H_n(Y^\vee)\right)'_b.

    The superscript ∨\vee means the complex-bilinear contragredient, including the multiplicity dual. The input consists of vectors in ⋂nℋn(Y)\bigcap_n\mathcal H_n(Y); it is not the contragredient test space. At a single positive label write Rp=(ℰp∨)b′R_p=(\mathscr E_p^\vee)'_b. Functorial entire-energy sources for positive Virasoro recipients, equations P.1–P.9.

    The meromorphic output ℳ\mathscr M consists of germs F(η)=η−1v+g(η)F(\eta)=\eta^{-1}v+g(\eta), with residue in the vacuum submodule and regular part bounded and holomorphic on one of the prescribed small discs in a weak Hilbert level space. Its level weights are e−mω(N)e^{-m\omega(N)}, where ω(N)=1+Np(N)\omega(N)=1+Np(N) and p(N)p(N) is the partition number; the disc and stage are allowed to shrink and weaken together. The topology is the original inductive-limit germ topology. Vacuum outputs are the spaces V(M)V(M) already defined.

    Now take closed Virasoro-invariant subspaces RR of finite products of these spaces, with their induced topologies. Morphisms are all ordinary continuous linear Virasoro intertwiners. Each factor keeps its original topology; “common” does not identify the different output spaces.

    First impose rapid decay for all positive-mode words. If qq is a continuous seminorm of RR, DD a finite Virasoro word, a>0a>0, and k≥0k\ge0, set

    pq,a,k,D(x)=∑n1,…,nk≥1ea(n1+⋯+nk)q(Ln1⋯LnkDx),p_{q,a,k,D}(x)= \sum_{n_1,\ldots,n_k\ge1} e^{a(n_1+\cdots+n_k)} q(L_{n_1}\cdots L_{n_k}Dx),

    where k=0k=0 means q(Dx)q(Dx). Let ℛreg(R)\mathcal R_{\mathrm{reg}}(R) be the space on which all these seminorms are finite. Full mode words are needed to justify successive meromorphic actions and their brackets.

    Let ZZ run through the elementary positive and vacuum outputs, with their original input spaces S0(Z)S_0(Z) and inclusions jZ:S0(Z)↪Zj_Z:S_0(Z)\hookrightarrow Z. Define

    𝒮com(R)={x∈ℛreg(R):Tx∈jZS0(Z) for every continuous Virasoro map T:R→Z}.\mathscr S_{\mathrm{com}}(R)= \left\{x\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{reg}}(R): Tx\in j_ZS_0(Z) \text{ for every continuous Virasoro map }T:R\to Z\right\}.

    Give it the regular-domain seminorms and every pulled-back seminorm of jZ−1Txj_Z^{-1}Tx. Testing all maps removes dependence on a chosen finite-product presentation.

    Theorem 10.2 (intrinsic complete sources). With these elementary spaces, their original topologies and the analytic hypotheses already stated, 𝒮com(R)\mathscr S_{\mathrm{com}}(R) is complete and Hausdorff and injects continuously and densely into RR. Every continuous Virasoro map restricts continuously to these sources. Meromorphic vector-field germs with finite principal part act by absolutely convergent mode series. On the elementary positive and vacuum objects the construction recovers the original topology exactly; in particular,

    𝒮com(Rp)=ℰp,𝒮com(V(M))=M⊗ˆπG.\mathscr S_{\mathrm{com}}(R_p) =\mathscr E_p, \qquad \mathscr S_{\mathrm{com}}(V(M)) =M\widehat\otimes_\pi G.

    An arbitrary common source need not be metrizable or nuclear. Complete functorial sources extending the original inputs, Theorems IS.1–IS.4.

    Completeness has a short explanation. In the complete product

    ℛreg(R)×∏(Z,T)S0(Z),\mathcal R_{\mathrm{reg}}(R)\times\prod_{(Z,T)}S_0(Z),

    impose the closed graph equations jZyZ,T=Txj_Zy_{Z,T}=Tx. Injectivity of jZj_Z determines every auxiliary coordinate. Precomposition with a morphism proves functoriality. Density needs more: scalar Fourier filters in L0L_0 converge to the identity in the output topology while mapping continuously into every required source. On the vacuum they fix Ω\Omega and cut off sufficiently high levels. The filters commute with intertwiners by their Fourier-integral construction; they are not themselves Virasoro intertwiners. Natural regularization on common Ward recipients, Theorems NR.3–NR.4.

    10.5 Collision and the two conditions for descent

    Exact recovery of the positive input spaces permits a decisive test. The prescribed structure constant has a two-sided Gaussian estimate, so for fixed a,b,z≠0a,b,z\ne0 there are C,D>0C,D>0 with

    C−1e−Dhp≤|gz(p)|≤CeDhp.C^{-1}e^{-Dh_p}\le |g_z(p)|\le Ce^{Dh_p}.

    Apply any fixed finite energy propagation e−τL0e^{-\tau L_0}, with τ∈ℂ\tau\in\mathbb C. The primary component becomes e−τhpgz(p)e^{-\tau h_p}g_z(p). Choosing an integer n>D+Re⁡τn>D+\operatorname{Re}\tau gives

    enhp|e−τhpgz(p)|≥C−1e(n−D−Re⁡τ)hp⟶∞.e^{nh_p}|e^{-\tau h_p}g_z(p)| \ge C^{-1}e^{(n-D-\operatorname{Re}\tau)h_p} \longrightarrow\infty.

    It fails an entire-energy seminorm. The corresponding spectral norm also diverges for the canonical measure. Both primary inputs belong to their prescribed source spaces, and their collision is a well-defined continuous output, but that output is outside the positive entire-energy source. Its positive projection is one of the tests in the definition of 𝒮com\mathscr S_{\mathrm{com}}, so the common construction cannot remove the failure. Entire positive sources and actual collision values, Theorem C.1.

    Multiplying by e−εL02e^{-\varepsilon L_0^2} does put the result into the positive source, but changes its primary coefficient and its covariance:

    e−εL02Lk=Lke−ε(L0−k)2.e^{-\varepsilon L_0^2}L_k =L_k e^{-\varepsilon(L_0-k)^2}.

    That regularized operation is useful on its stated domain. It is a different operation.

    There is nevertheless a complete source attached to each actual finite sewing. If μ:E→R\mu:E\to R is the sewn map, its exact quotient T=E/ker⁡μT=E/\ker\mu is complete Fréchet and has a continuous injective dense realization j:T→μ(E)j:T\to\overline{\mu(E)}. The quotient topology can be strictly finer than the topology induced from RR. This distinction separates two obligations for a proposed continuous linear composite map F:E→WF:E\to W:

    1. It must annihilate the actual kernel, F(ker⁡μ)=0F(\ker\mu)=0, so that its value depends only on the sewn vector.
    2. The induced map on μ(E)\mu(E) must be continuous for the topology inherited from RR, if it is to extend continuously to the completed image in RR.

    For complete Hausdorff WW, these conditions give the unique continuous extension from the dense image. Continuity of FF on EE gives continuity on the quotient source; it does not by itself give the second condition. Ward identities likewise do not replace the first. Rational Ward identities and quotient sources for finite sewings, Corollary FWd.3 and §“What the quotient property represents”.

    On the completed binary sources with a vacuum factor, source separation proves injectivity of the actual continuous linear field maps on their stated received stages. The argument extracts a nonzero finite-bidegree component of a hypothetical kernel vector, then uses positive-mode words to reach the tensor of highest vectors, whose field value is nonzero. Even zero kernel does not make the image topology equal to the source topology or produce a continuous inverse. Injectivity with completed vacuum inputs, Lemma KV.1 and Theorems KV.3–KV.5.

    Finite cluster sewings and their reassociation maps remain defined with their proper input stages. The outstanding tensor-category question asks for composite domains on which the original operations satisfy these two descent conditions, retain the coefficient-one units, and agree with the proved changes of parentheses. A numerical state poses a further question: after an output has been constructed, what evaluates it, and what normalization or line does that evaluation retain? This is the question of the next chapter.

    11

    States, determinant lines and quantum fields

    For λ,ℏ>0\lambda,\hbar>0, the Gaussian integral and its normalized second moment are

    Zλ(1)=∫ℝe−λx2/(2ℏ)dx=2πℏλ,Zλ(x2)Zλ(1)=ℏλ.Z_\lambda(1)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\lambda x^2/(2\hbar)}\,dx =\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\hbar}{\lambda}}, \qquad \frac{Z_\lambda(x^2)}{Z_\lambda(1)}=\frac{\hbar}{\lambda}.

    Multiplying the measure by any nonzero constant changes the first expression and leaves the second unchanged. A normalized state therefore cannot recover the normalization of the integral that produced it. In a family of complex field theories, it also cannot recover the choice of integration cycle or its phase.

    This distinction persists after all the analytic difficulties of the Gaussian have been solved. A convergent normalized state, a renormalized determinant line, and a state prepared by a geometric filling are different mathematical objects. The quadratic gravity construction supplies the first and a local form of the second on specified domains. Its relation to a physical cap requires additional maps, boundary conditions and gluing laws. We shall develop the finite action first, because it fixes the signs and normalizations that survive every later limit.
